meta.blurb: A boy lifts a rock and finds his father's sword and sandals beneath it. Plutarch tells the lives of Greeks and Romans, from Theseus to Cleopatra's golden barge, and shows how small stories reveal a person's character.
meta.bible: Plutarch: a Greek writer and priest of Delphi, born in Chaeronea about AD 46; he wrote paired lives of Greeks and Romans; he cares more about character than about battles, and often tells small stories and says when something is only a legend. Chaeronea: his home town in Greece. Delphi: the temple of Apollo where Plutarch served as priest. Theseus: the legendary hero-king of Athens. Aegeus: his father. Minos: the king of Crete. Minotaur: the monster in the labyrinth. Ariadne: the daughter of Minos who gave Theseus a thread. Crete: the island. Labyrinth: a maze. Romulus: the legendary founder of Rome; Remus: his twin brother. Amulius: the wicked king of Alba. Faustulus: the shepherd who found the twins. Lycurgus: the lawgiver of Sparta. Solon: the wise lawgiver of Athens. Aristides: the Athenian called the Just. Themistocles: the Athenian who won at Salamis. Eurybiades: the Spartan commander of the Greek fleet. Pericles: the leader of Athens in its golden age. Anaxagoras: his teacher. Pheidias: the great sculptor. Alcibiades: the brilliant, reckless young Athenian. Socrates: the philosopher. Demosthenes: the great Athenian speaker. Philip: the king of Macedon. Alexander: Philip's son, Alexander the Great. Bucephalus: his horse. Aristotle: his teacher. Diogenes: the philosopher who lived in a barrel. Darius: the Persian king beaten by Alexander. Porus: an Indian king. Cato: the stern Roman, called the Elder. Fabius: the Roman who wore Hannibal down by delay. Hannibal: the general from Carthage. Pyrrhus: the king of Epirus. Coriolanus: the proud Roman who turned on Rome. Volumnia: his mother. Volscians: Rome's enemies. Julius Caesar: the Roman general and dictator. Pompey: his rival. Cleopatra: the queen of Egypt. Brutus and Cassius: two of Caesar's killers. Cicero: the Roman speaker and writer. Catiline: the traitor Cicero exposed. Mark Antony: the Roman soldier who loved Cleopatra. Octavian: Caesar's heir, later Augustus. Calpurnia: Caesar's wife. Senate: the council of Rome. Consul: a chief officer of Rome. Orator: a public speaker. Ostracism: a vote in which Athenians could send a man into exile for ten years. Legend: a story that may not be true. Athens, Sparta, Rome, Greece, Macedon, Persia, Egypt, Alexandria, Babylon, Carthage, Italy, Salamis, Marathon, Parthenon, Acropolis, Rubicon, Pharsalus, Philippi, Actium, the Nile, Corioli, Tarsus: the places. Dates are about: Rome's traditional founding 753 BC, Salamis 480 BC, Pericles dies 429 BC, Alexander dies 323 BC, Caesar dies 44 BC, Actium 31 BC. Voice and tone: wise, warm and curious, a storyteller with a moral eye; deaths are stated plainly, without gore. More names and facts (chapters 14 to 20): Gaius Marcius Coriolanus: a proud Roman, exiled about the early fifth century BC; Virgilia: his wife; Menenius Agrippa: the senator whose fable of the belly calmed the poor; Cominius: the consul at Corioli; Tullus Aufidius: the Volscian general; Antium: the Volscian city; tribunes: officers who protect the poor. Cineas: the wise adviser of Pyrrhus; Tarentum: the Greek city that called Pyrrhus to Italy; Heraclea 280 BC and Asculum 279 BC: his two costly wins; Fabricius: the honest Roman envoy; Quintus Fabius Maximus: called the Lamb as a boy and later the Delayer; Minucius: his deputy; Lake Trasimene 217 BC and Cannae 216 BC: Roman defeats by Hannibal; Fabius dies in 203 BC. Marcus Porcius Cato: born about 234 BC, consul 195 BC, censor 184 BC, dies 149 BC; Valerius Flaccus: his noble neighbour; Antiochus: the king beaten at Thermopylae in 191 BC; Scipio Nasica: Cato's rival who wished Carthage spared; Carthage is destroyed in 146 BC. Caesar's pirates: he is ransomed for fifty talents; Crassus: the richest Roman, killed fighting the Parthians; Julia: Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, dies in 54 BC; Ptolemy: Cleopatra's young brother; Apollodorus: the servant who carried her in a bed-sack; Pharnaces and Zela: the king beaten in 47 BC (I came, I saw, I conquered); Lupercalia: the festival where Antony offered the crown; Spurinna: the soothsayer; Decimus Brutus: a plotter; Abydos: where the ghost came to Brutus; Octavia: Octavian's sister, married to Antony; Fulvia: Antony's earlier wife; Lepidus: the third man with Antony and Octavian; Parthians: the enemies in the east; Clodius: Cicero's enemy; Tullia: Cicero's daughter; Verres: the corrupt governor of Sicily; Arpinum: Cicero's home town; Philippics: Cicero's speeches against Antony; Sir Thomas North: translated Plutarch into English in 1579.

The Golden Boy and His Dog

beats.scene: Plutarch writes on a scroll in a quiet room at Delphi
beats.summary: Plutarch explains that he writes lives, not histories, because small acts show character.

beats.scene: Small stone houses climb a green hillside in Greece
beats.summary: Plutarch is born about AD 46 in Chaeronea, a small town in Greece, and stays there for most of his life.

beats.scene: Young men listen to a teacher in a shaded colonnade
beats.summary: As a young man Plutarch studies philosophy in Athens under the teacher Ammonius.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a paved road toward a distant city of marble
beats.summary: Greece belongs to the Roman empire, and Plutarch visits Rome, lectures there and makes powerful friends.

beats.scene: Pilgrims climb a steep stone path to a temple on a mountain
beats.summary: Plutarch becomes a priest of Apollo at Delphi, where visitors come from far away to question the god.

beats.scene: Two scrolls lie side by side on a wooden desk
beats.summary: Plutarch plans to write famous lives in pairs, one Greek and one Roman, so the reader can compare them.

beats.scene: A painter studies a man's face with a brush in his hand
beats.summary: Plutarch compares himself to a portrait painter who takes most care over the face and the eyes.

beats.scene: Two men laugh over a cup while a battle map lies unrolled
beats.summary: A short saying or a joke, Plutarch says, can show more of a man than a battle with thousands of dead.

beats.scene: A mapmaker draws the edge of a map and adds wild beasts
beats.summary: Plutarch says that, like mapmakers, he will mark where history ends and legend begins.

beats.scene: A man holds up a mirror and studies his own face
beats.summary: Plutarch says he began writing lives for others but kept writing them as a mirror for himself.

beats.scene: A boy stands beside an old king in a stone courtyard
beats.summary: Theseus grows up in Troezen with his mother and grandfather, far from his father Aegeus, king of Athens.

beats.scene: Boys run from a lion skin while one boy lifts an axe
beats.summary: When Hercules visits, the boys flee from his lion skin, but seven-year-old Theseus snatches up an axe.

beats.scene: A young man lifts a huge rock and finds a sword under it
beats.summary: At sixteen Theseus lifts the rock that hides his father's sword and sandals.

beats.scene: A young man turns from a ship toward a rough mountain road
beats.summary: Theseus ignores the safe sea route to Athens and takes the dangerous road by land, as Hercules would have done.

beats.scene: A young man faces a giant robber with a heavy iron club
beats.summary: Theseus kills the robber Periphetes and keeps his club.

beats.scene: A huge pine tree bent to the ground with a robber standing near
beats.summary: Theseus defeats Sinis, who bent pine trees to the ground, with the very trick Sinis used on others.

beats.scene: A young man stands on a cliff edge above the sea facing a robber
beats.summary: Theseus kills the wild sow of Crommyon and throws the cliff robber Sciron into the sea.

beats.scene: A young wrestler stands beside an iron bed in a dark house
beats.summary: Theseus beats the wrestler Cercyon at Eleusis and then forces Procrustes to fit his own iron bed.

beats.scene: A tired young traveller in a dusty cloak enters the gates of a city
beats.summary: Theseus is cleansed at the river Cephisus, enters Athens in secret and finds Medea ruling the old king's mind.

beats.scene: An old king knocks a cup from a young man's hand
beats.summary: Medea tries to poison Theseus at a banquet, but Aegeus sees the sword and dashes the cup away.

beats.scene: A young man holds a huge wild bull by the horns on a plain
beats.summary: Theseus defeats the plot of his cousins, the Pallantids, and captures the wild bull of Marathon.

beats.scene: A crowd on a quay watches young people board a ship
beats.summary: Athens must send seven young men and seven young women to Crete, and Theseus offers to go.

beats.scene: An old king gives a white cloth to his son at the harbour
beats.summary: The ship sails under a black sail, and Aegeus gives Theseus a white sail to raise if he lives.

beats.scene: A girl hands a ball of thread to a young man
beats.summary: In Crete, Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, falls in love with Theseus and gives him a ball of thread.

beats.scene: Theseus walks a dark maze unwinding a thread from a girl
beats.summary: Theseus enters the Labyrinth of Crete and kills the Minotaur, then follows the thread out.

beats.scene: A ship sails away from an island at night with young people on deck
beats.summary: Theseus and the young Athenians escape from Crete, and the old writers tell different stories about it.

beats.scene: Young people dance in a winding line on a sandy beach
beats.summary: On the island of Delos, Theseus leads the young people in a winding dance that copies the Labyrinth.

beats.scene: An old king on a cliff watches a ship with a black sail
beats.summary: Theseus forgets the white sail, and Aegeus, believing his son dead, throws himself into the sea.

beats.scene: Villagers from many villages gather in a city square under one banner
beats.summary: As king, Theseus unites the villages of Attica into one city, Athens.

beats.scene: Soldiers carry old bones in a bronze coffin onto a ship
beats.summary: Theseus dies far from home on Scyros, and about 475 BC Cimon brings his bones back to Athens.

beats.scene: A wicked king sits on a throne while an old man stands aside
beats.summary: Amulius seizes the throne of Alba Longa from his brother Numitor, and Numitor's daughter Rhea Silvia bears twin boys.

beats.scene: A wooden trough floats on a flooded river
beats.summary: Amulius orders the twins to be left to the river Tiber, but the flood carries them gently ashore.

beats.scene: A she-wolf feeds two baby boys beside a river
beats.summary: A she-wolf feeds the twins and a woodpecker brings them food, until the shepherd Faustulus finds them.

beats.scene: Young shepherds fight with sticks beside a stream
beats.summary: The twins grow up as brave leaders of the shepherds, and Remus is captured in a quarrel with Numitor's herdsmen.

beats.scene: Two young men stand before an old king in a hall
beats.summary: The twins learn who they are, overthrow Amulius and give the throne back to their grandfather Numitor.

beats.scene: Two brothers watch birds in the sky from two hills
beats.summary: The brothers quarrel over the site of the city and watch for vultures, and each claims the sign.

beats.scene: A boy jumps over a low wall while his brother stares
beats.summary: Romulus ploughs a furrow for his wall, Remus mocks it and leaps over it, and Remus is killed.

beats.scene: Crowds of young men rush into a festival crowd
beats.summary: Romulus fills Rome with outcasts, and because Rome lacks women the Romans carry off Sabine women at a festival.

beats.scene: Women run between two armies with their hair loose
beats.summary: Titus Tatius and the Sabines attack Rome, but the women run between the armies and make peace.

beats.scene: A dark storm cloud covers a field of soldiers while a king vanishes
beats.summary: Romulus rules alone after Tatius dies, then vanishes in a storm, and Proculus says he has become a god.

beats.scene: A tall man holds up a baby before a crowd in a hall
beats.summary: When his brother the king dies, Lycurgus refuses the throne and shows the Spartans their baby king.

beats.scene: A traveller sits with an old poet and a pile of scrolls
beats.summary: Lycurgus leaves Sparta, studies the laws of Crete and Asia and brings back the poems of Homer.

beats.scene: A man kneels at a temple while a priestess speaks
beats.summary: The Spartans beg Lycurgus to return, and at Delphi the priestess calls him dear to the gods.

beats.scene: Old men sit in a stone circle voting while a crowd shouts
beats.summary: Lycurgus creates a council of twenty-eight elders to balance the power of the kings and the people.

beats.scene: Surveyors measure a wide field into equal plots
beats.summary: Lycurgus divides the land of Laconia into equal lots, so that no Spartan family is very rich or very poor.

beats.scene: A young man holds his hand over his eye in an angry crowd
beats.summary: A hot-tempered young man named Alcander blinds one of Lycurgus's eyes, and Lycurgus answers him with kindness.

beats.scene: An ox cart carries a heap of heavy iron bars
beats.summary: Lycurgus bans gold and silver and makes Sparta's money from heavy iron, so that hoarding and stealing are useless.

beats.scene: Spartan men sit at long tables sharing plain food
beats.summary: Lycurgus makes every citizen eat at a common table, where the black broth is famous and the rich cannot show off.

beats.scene: A boy stands stiffly with a cloak over a hidden fox
beats.summary: Spartan boys are trained from the age of seven to bear hunger, cold and pain, and one hides a stolen fox rather than be caught.

beats.scene: An old man looks toward the sea from the deck of a ship
beats.summary: Lycurgus makes the Spartans swear to keep his laws until he returns, then never comes back, and Sparta keeps his laws for centuries.

beats.scene: A poet reads verses aloud in a busy harbour market
beats.summary: Solon, a poet and merchant from an old but poor family, travels widely and writes verse.

beats.scene: A man in a felt cap recites a poem in the market
beats.summary: Athens has banned any talk of retaking Salamis, so Solon pretends to be mad and stirs the people with a poem.

beats.scene: Poor farmers kneel before rich men beside stone boundary markers
beats.summary: Many poor Athenians owe the rich and lose their farms and even their freedom, and the city nears civil war.

beats.scene: A poor farmer hands a tablet to a rich man in Athens
beats.summary: The Athenians choose Solon about 594 BC, and he cancels the debts crushing the poor, in the shaking-off of burdens.

beats.scene: Men step from a ship into the arms of their families
beats.summary: Solon frees Athenians enslaved for debt and brings home citizens who were sold abroad.

beats.scene: Four groups of citizens stand around a stone platform
beats.summary: Solon divides the citizens into four classes by wealth and gives even the poorest a vote.

beats.scene: Solon speaks to a crowd beside wooden tablets covered in laws
beats.summary: Solon writes his laws on wooden tablets, including a rule against standing aside in a civil quarrel.

beats.scene: A lone man stands on the deck of a ship leaving a harbour
beats.summary: Tired of being asked to change his laws, Solon leaves Athens for ten years and travels to Egypt and Cyprus.

beats.scene: A king on a golden throne listens to a plainly dressed traveller
beats.summary: In Lydia Solon tells the rich King Croesus that no one can be called happy until his life is over.

beats.scene: A man with bandages rides a mule cart into a busy market
beats.summary: Peisistratus wounds himself, tricks the Athenians into giving him bodyguards and makes himself tyrant; Solon dies about 560 BC.

beats.scene: A man in a plain cloak settles a quarrel between two neighbours
beats.summary: Aristides earns the name the Just, stays poor, and at Marathon in 490 BC gives up his turn at command to Miltiades.

beats.scene: A farmer asks a calm man to write a name on a pottery shard
beats.summary: The Athenians vote to exile Aristides by ostracism, and a farmer who cannot write asks Aristides himself to write the name.

beats.scene: Workers build warships on a beach under a hot sun
beats.summary: The victory of Miltiades at Marathon haunts Themistocles, who persuades Athens to spend the silver of Laurium on a fleet.

beats.scene: Families carry bundles aboard boats while the city stands empty
beats.summary: Xerxes marches on Greece in 480 BC, Delphi speaks of a wooden wall, and Themistocles says it means ships, so the Athenians leave the city.

beats.scene: A Spartan raises a stick at Themistocles on a warship
beats.summary: At Salamis, when the Spartan commander Eurybiades raises his stick, Themistocles says, Strike me, but listen to me.

beats.scene: A man slips through a harbour full of enemy ships at night
beats.summary: Themistocles tricks Xerxes into closing the strait, and the exile Aristides slips through the Persian ships to warn that the Greeks are surrounded.

beats.scene: A narrow strait packed with ships, with a king watching from a throne
beats.summary: At Salamis in 480 BC the crowded Persian fleet is beaten, and Xerxes, who watched from a throne, begins the journey home.

beats.scene: Citizens carry a plain coffin while two young women follow
beats.summary: Aristides leads the Athenians at Plataea in 479 BC, sets fair payments for the allies and dies so poor that Athens pays for his daughters' weddings.

beats.scene: A crowd in a stadium turns to look at one man
beats.summary: The Greeks honour Themistocles, but Athens grows jealous, ostracises him and then accuses him of treason, and he flees.

beats.scene: A traveller in a hood arrives in a Persian court
beats.summary: Themistocles reaches Persia, learns the language, is welcomed by Artaxerxes and dies at Magnesia around 460 BC.

beats.scene: Pericles stands tall on a platform with a plumed helmet and speaks
beats.summary: Pericles, a noble with an oddly long head, is shown in statues wearing a helmet and is known for his unshakable calm.

beats.scene: A philosopher and a fortune-teller argue over a ram with one horn
beats.summary: Pericles learns calm and clear thinking from Anaxagoras, and a one-horned ram is explained in two ways.

beats.scene: A lone man walks along a street toward the council hall
beats.summary: Pericles refuses invitations to dinners and walks only the road to the market and the council, which makes people trust him.

beats.scene: Citizens file into a court as an official hands out coins
beats.summary: Pericles introduces pay for jurors, so that poor citizens can take a real part in the government.

beats.scene: Workers raise white marble columns on the Acropolis in sunlight
beats.summary: Pericles builds the Parthenon and the other great works of Athens, which give work to thousands.

beats.scene: A giant gold and ivory statue of Athena stands in a workshop
beats.summary: The sculptor Pheidias, who directs the works and makes the great statue of Athena, is accused by Pericles's enemies and dies in prison.

beats.scene: A man kisses a woman at a doorway as he leaves for work
beats.summary: Pericles loves Aspasia, a clever woman of Miletus whom even Socrates comes to hear, and he defends her in court.

beats.scene: Crowded streets of Athens in a hot summer with people sick
beats.summary: War with Sparta begins in 431 BC, Pericles brings the country people inside the walls, and a plague strikes crowded Athens.

beats.scene: A man places a wreath on a young man's coffin and weeps
beats.summary: Pericles loses both his legitimate sons to the plague, weeps at the funeral of Paralus, and is elected general again.

beats.scene: Pericles lies in bed as his friends talk quietly around him
beats.summary: Pericles dies in 429 BC, proud that no Athenian wore mourning because of him.

beats.scene: A boy lies in the road in front of a loaded cart
beats.summary: Alcibiades, handsome and spoiled, is raised in the house of Pericles and lies down in the road to stop a cart.

beats.scene: Two boys wrestle in a ring while a crowd watches
beats.summary: Alcibiades bites a stronger wrestler, says he bites like a lion, and refuses to learn the flute because it twists the face.

beats.scene: Two men talk on a street while a crowd watches
beats.summary: Many flatter Alcibiades, but only Socrates can make him blush and weep, though the young man keeps running away.

beats.scene: Alcibiades walks through the Athenian market with a dog behind him
beats.summary: Alcibiades cuts the tail from his beautiful dog so that Athens will talk about that and nothing worse.

beats.scene: A soldier shields a wounded friend on a battlefield
beats.summary: At Potidaea Socrates saves Alcibiades, and later at Delium Alcibiades rides beside Socrates to protect him.

beats.scene: Greek ships sail to Sicily as a young man waves from the deck
beats.summary: Alcibiades argues against the cautious Nicias and persuades Athens to attack Sicily in 415 BC.

beats.scene: Broken marble statues lie in a street at dawn
beats.summary: The stone heads of Hermes are smashed in one night, Alcibiades is accused and, ordered home to trial, he escapes.

beats.scene: A man in a plain Spartan cloak eats black broth at a long table
beats.summary: Alcibiades goes to Sparta, adopts its hard ways and advises the Spartans how to hurt Athens.

beats.scene: A ship enters a harbour greeted by a cheering crowd with garlands
beats.summary: After winning victories at sea, Alcibiades returns to Athens in triumph in 407 BC.

beats.scene: A burning house at night as a man steps out with a sword
beats.summary: After a defeat at Notium Alcibiades is blamed and exiled again, and he is killed in Phrygia in 404 BC.

beats.scene: A young man speaks in a law court before a row of jurors
beats.summary: Demosthenes loses his father at seven, his guardians waste his fortune, and he takes them to court.

beats.scene: A young man walks away from a platform while a crowd laughs
beats.summary: Demosthenes' first speech to the assembly fails, and the actor Satyrus shows him how much voice and gesture matter.

beats.scene: Demosthenes practises speaking with pebbles in his mouth by the sea
beats.summary: Demosthenes overcomes a stammer with pebbles in his mouth, verses recited uphill and shouting into the waves.

beats.scene: A young man with half a shaved head studies by lamplight in a cellar
beats.summary: Demosthenes builds an underground study and shaves half his head so that shame keeps him at his work.

beats.scene: Demosthenes speaks to a crowded assembly while Macedonian envoys listen
beats.summary: Philip of Macedon grows stronger every year, and Demosthenes warns Athens against him in speeches called the Philippics.

beats.scene: Envoys from Athens and Thebes clasp hands in a hall
beats.summary: When Philip marches south, Demosthenes persuades Thebes to join Athens against him.

beats.scene: Two armies clash on a plain below a hill at Chaeronea
beats.summary: In 338 BC Philip and Alexander defeat the Greeks at Chaeronea, Plutarch's own town, and Greek freedom ends.

beats.scene: A man tells a fable to a crowd about sheep, dogs and wolves
beats.summary: After Thebes falls, Alexander demands the leading Athenian speakers, and Demosthenes tells the fable of the wolves and the sheepdogs.

beats.scene: A man in a small boat crosses stormy water toward an island
beats.summary: After Alexander dies in 323 BC, Athens rebels, Antipater wins, and Demosthenes is condemned and flees.

beats.scene: An old man stands in a temple holding a reed pen
beats.summary: On Calauria Demosthenes takes poison from his pen rather than be captured, and dies in 322 BC.

beats.scene: A queen holds a newborn baby in a palace beside a Macedonian king
beats.summary: Alexander is born in 356 BC to King Philip of Macedon and Queen Olympias, who claim descent from Hercules and Achilles.

beats.scene: A boy frowns as his father's soldiers return from another victory
beats.summary: As a boy Alexander is quick and ambitious, and each time Philip wins a city he fears that nothing great will be left for him.

beats.scene: A boy turns a black horse toward the sun to calm it
beats.summary: The boy Alexander tames the horse Bucephalus by turning it away from its own shadow, and Philip tells him to find a bigger kingdom.

beats.scene: Aristotle teaches young Alexander under a tree on a hillside
beats.summary: Philip hires Aristotle to teach Alexander at Mieza, and Alexander learns to love books, above all Homer.

beats.scene: A boy asks questions of foreign visitors in rich robes
beats.summary: When Persian envoys visit, young Alexander asks them about the roads into Asia and the character of their king.

beats.scene: A young prince on horseback leads a cavalry charge
beats.summary: At eighteen Alexander leads the cavalry at Chaeronea and is the first to break the Sacred Band of Thebes.

beats.scene: A young man throws a cup across a wedding table
beats.summary: At Philip's second wedding Attalus insults Alexander, who throws his cup, and Philip draws his sword but falls over drunk.

beats.scene: A king lies fallen at the entrance of a theatre
beats.summary: Philip is murdered in 336 BC by the bodyguard Pausanias, and Alexander becomes king at twenty.

beats.scene: A burning city with one house left untouched
beats.summary: Thebes revolts in 335 BC, and Alexander destroys it but spares the temples and the house of the poet Pindar.

beats.scene: Alexander stands in front of Diogenes lying in the sun by his barrel
beats.summary: At Corinth the Greeks make Alexander their leader against Persia, and the philosopher Diogenes asks him to stand out of his sun.

beats.scene: A young king signs deeds while friends smile and take land
beats.summary: Before crossing to Asia in 334 BC, Alexander gives away most of his property, and when Perdiccas asks what he keeps, he says hope.

beats.scene: A young king lays a wreath on an ancient tomb
beats.summary: At Troy Alexander honours the tomb of Achilles and says that Achilles was lucky to have Homer to proclaim his fame.

beats.scene: Horsemen splash across a river under a rain of arrows
beats.summary: At the Granicus river in 334 BC Alexander attacks across the water, and his friend Cleitus saves his life.

beats.scene: Alexander draws his sword against a huge knot on an old cart
beats.summary: At Gordium Alexander cuts the knot that was said to give the rule of Asia to whoever could undo it.

beats.scene: Persian women bow before Alexander in a royal tent
beats.summary: Alexander routs Darius at Issus in 333 BC and treats the captured Persian royal family with great respect.

beats.scene: Soldiers build a stone causeway toward a walled island city
beats.summary: Alexander besieges the island city of Tyre in 332 BC and builds a causeway across the sea until it falls.

beats.scene: Soldiers mark the outline of a city with flour as birds descend
beats.summary: In Egypt Alexander marks out the city of Alexandria with barley meal, and birds eat it, which the seers call a good sign.

beats.scene: Travellers walk across a desert toward a temple among palm trees
beats.summary: Alexander crosses the desert to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa, where the priest greets him as the son of the god.

beats.scene: A commander sleeps in his tent at dawn while officers wait outside
beats.summary: Before the battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC Alexander sleeps so soundly that Parmenio must wake him.

beats.scene: Flames rise from a great stone palace in the night as people watch
beats.summary: Alexander seizes Babylon, Susa and Persepolis, and at Persepolis a drunken feast ends with the palace on fire.

beats.scene: A king hands back a helmet of water while soldiers watch
beats.summary: In the chase of Darius through the desert, soldiers offer Alexander a helmet of water, and he refuses to drink alone.

beats.scene: A conqueror covers a dying king's body with his own cloak
beats.summary: Bessus and other nobles murder Darius, and Alexander covers his body with his own cloak and has him buried with honour.

beats.scene: A feast table is overturned as a king stares in shock
beats.summary: At a drunken banquet in 328 BC Alexander kills his friend Cleitus, who had saved his life, and in grief refuses food for days.

beats.scene: A tall Indian king stands before Alexander near a river bank
beats.summary: At the Hydaspes in 326 BC Alexander defeats King Porus, who asks to be treated like a king.

beats.scene: A king stands beside a fallen black horse near a river
beats.summary: Bucephalus dies after the battle with Porus, and Alexander founds a city in his name.

beats.scene: Weary soldiers sit on a river bank as the king looks east
beats.summary: At the Hyphasis the exhausted army refuses to go farther into India, and Alexander gives way and turns back.

beats.scene: Soldiers carry a wounded king on a shield
beats.summary: Sailing down the rivers of India, Alexander is badly wounded by an arrow in a town of the Malli but recovers.

beats.scene: Tired soldiers cross hot sand dunes in a long line
beats.summary: On the return through the Gedrosian desert, many in Alexander's army die of thirst and heat.

beats.scene: Many couples in Greek and Persian dress stand under a huge tent
beats.summary: At Susa in 324 BC Alexander marries a Persian princess and weds his officers to Persian women, but soon his dearest friend Hephaestion dies.

beats.scene: Alexander lies sick in a palace in Babylon as soldiers file past
beats.summary: Alexander dies in Babylon in June 323 BC at thirty-two and, asked who should have his kingdom, says the strongest.

beats.scene: A widow in a Roman house watches her young son train with weapons
beats.summary: Gaius Marcius is raised by his widowed mother Volumnia and grows into a brave, proud and rough soldier.

beats.scene: Poor Romans walk out of the city gates and camp on a hill
beats.summary: The poor of Rome, angry about debt, leave the city, and the wise Menenius persuades them to return with his fable of the belly.

beats.scene: A soldier fights alone inside the gates of an enemy town
beats.summary: In the siege of the Volscian city of Corioli, Marcius rushes through the gates alone and the Romans follow and take the city.

beats.scene: A consul crowns a soldier and offers him a share of treasure
beats.summary: The consul gives Marcius the surname Coriolanus and a rich reward, but he takes only a horse and asks freedom for one prisoner.

beats.scene: A proud man in a plain white robe shows scars to a crowd
beats.summary: Coriolanus stands for the consulship, but he shows his scars with a poor grace and the voters reject him.

beats.scene: Grain sacks arrive at a Roman harbour while an angry crowd waits
beats.summary: In a famine Coriolanus argues that the poor should not get cheap grain unless the tribunes lose their power, and the tribunes bring him to trial.

beats.scene: A man in a cloak embraces his mother and wife at a Roman gate
beats.summary: Condemned to exile, Coriolanus calmly says goodbye to his mother and wife and leaves Rome with only a few friends.

beats.scene: A stranger sits quietly by a fire in an enemy general's house
beats.summary: Coriolanus goes to the Volscian leader Tullus Aufidius, an old enemy, and offers him his sword against Rome.

beats.scene: An army camps outside Rome while envoys in robes walk toward the tents
beats.summary: A Volscian army led by Coriolanus camps near Rome, and the envoys and priests sent to him are turned away.

beats.scene: A mother kneels before her son in a camp, with his wife and children
beats.summary: Volumnia and the Roman women plead with Coriolanus, and he yields, saying she has saved Rome but lost her son.

beats.scene: A king in a plumed helmet talks with a wise adviser at a table
beats.summary: Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, prepares to fight Rome, and his adviser Cineas asks what he will do when he has won.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers stare in fear at huge grey animals on a plain
beats.summary: At Heraclea in 280 BC the Romans meet war elephants for the first time, and Pyrrhus wins, though he loses many men.

beats.scene: A plain Roman envoy stands calmly before a king and a curtain
beats.summary: Fabricius, the Roman envoy, refuses Pyrrhus's gold and is not frightened when an elephant appears behind a curtain.

beats.scene: A king looks over a field of the dead and shakes his head
beats.summary: After another costly win at Asculum, Pyrrhus says that one more such victory would ruin him, and he leaves Italy.

beats.scene: A gentle boy stands in a Roman field among his sheep
beats.summary: Fabius Maximus, a calm and patient man nicknamed the Lamb as a boy, is chosen to lead Rome when Hannibal crosses the Alps.

beats.scene: A Roman general watches an enemy camp from a distant hill
beats.summary: Fabius follows Hannibal's army but refuses to fight a great battle, and the Romans mock him and call him the slow one.

beats.scene: Hundreds of oxen with burning torches on their horns run across hills at night
beats.summary: Hannibal is trapped in a valley, but he escapes at night by driving oxen with burning torches on their horns up the hillsides.

beats.scene: A general in a plain cloak embraces a younger officer on a hillside
beats.summary: Minucius, Fabius's deputy, is given equal power by the angry people, nearly loses his army, and is saved by Fabius.

beats.scene: A broken Roman army lies on a hot plain under a red sky
beats.summary: At Cannae in 216 BC the Romans fight Hannibal in open battle against Fabius's advice and are crushed, which proves him right.

beats.scene: Roman citizens drop small coins into a basket beside a funeral bed
beats.summary: Fabius sells his own land to ransom prisoners, lives to an old age and dies in 203 BC, and the Romans pay for his funeral.

beats.scene: A farmer in plain clothes digs a field beside his workers
beats.summary: Cato the Elder, born about 234 BC in the country, works his own farm, eats simple food and dresses like his workers.

beats.scene: A young soldier in a plain helmet marches with a Roman column
beats.summary: Cato serves as a young soldier in the war against Hannibal and shows a hardy spirit.

beats.scene: A farmer stands up before a crowded Roman law court
beats.summary: A noble neighbour, Valerius Flaccus, urges Cato to go into public life, and his speeches in court make him famous.

beats.scene: A Roman consul commands his army before a walled Spanish town
beats.summary: Elected consul in 195 BC, Cato goes to Spain, wins the tribes over and returns to a triumph in Rome.

beats.scene: Soldiers climb a rocky mountain path above a narrow pass at dawn
beats.summary: At Thermopylae in 191 BC Cato leads a force over the mountain and attacks the king's army from behind.

beats.scene: A stern official in a toga strikes names from a long list
beats.summary: As censor in 184 BC Cato judges the conduct of Romans, expels a senator, taxes luxuries and makes enemies.

beats.scene: A white-haired senator frowns at a group of Greek philosophers in robes
beats.summary: When Athenian philosophers visit Rome in 155 BC and charm the young, Cato asks the Senate to send them home.

beats.scene: A man opens his toga and drops ripe figs on a senate floor
beats.summary: Returning from an embassy to Carthage, Cato shows the senators ripe figs and says the land that grew them is three days away.

beats.scene: An old senator lifts one finger in a crowded Roman council
beats.summary: From then on Cato ends every speech by saying that Carthage must be destroyed, while Scipio Nasica says it should be spared.

beats.scene: An old man writes at a desk beside piles of scrolls
beats.summary: Cato dies in 149 BC at about eighty-five, and Carthage is destroyed three years later.

beats.scene: A young Roman stands calmly on a pirate ship among rough sailors
beats.summary: Young Julius Caesar is captured by pirates near Greece, laughs that they ask too little ransom and tells them to ask for more.

beats.scene: A prisoner reads aloud to a ring of listening pirates
beats.summary: For about forty days Caesar lives among the pirates as if he were their leader, joking, exercising and reading them his speeches.

beats.scene: A line of Roman warships chases a pirate vessel across a bright sea
beats.summary: When the ransom is paid Caesar raises ships at once, catches the pirates and has them punished, as he had promised.

beats.scene: A young man weeps over an old scroll about a conqueror
beats.summary: In Spain Caesar reads about Alexander and weeps, because at his own age Alexander had conquered so much.

beats.scene: Three men in togas clasp hands at a table in a Roman house
beats.summary: Caesar joins the powerful Pompey and the rich Crassus in an alliance, becomes consul in 59 BC, and wins command in Gaul.

beats.scene: A general rides before soldiers who march through a rainy forest
beats.summary: In about eight years of war in Gaul, Caesar conquers the country, bridges the Rhine and crosses to Britain, loved by his soldiers.

beats.scene: A shrouded body lies at a funeral while two generals stand apart
beats.summary: After Crassus and Caesar's daughter Julia die, the alliance breaks, and the Senate orders Caesar to give up his army.

beats.scene: A general on horseback stops at a small river at dawn
beats.summary: In January 49 BC Caesar hesitates at the Rubicon, then crosses with his army, saying, “Let the die be cast.”

beats.scene: Cavalry and foot soldiers clash on a dry plain beneath a hot sun
beats.summary: At Pharsalus in Greece in 48 BC Caesar, with a much smaller army, defeats Pompey, who flees.

beats.scene: A grieving general turns away from a messenger holding out a cloth bundle
beats.summary: Pompey is murdered as he lands in Egypt, and when Caesar arrives and is shown his head, he weeps.

beats.scene: A servant carries a long bundle through palace gates at night
beats.summary: In Alexandria the young Cleopatra has herself carried secretly to Caesar in a bed-sack, and he is charmed by her.

beats.scene: A general in a dusty tent writes a short note by lamplight
beats.summary: Caesar wins the Alexandrian war and then defeats a king at Zela in 47 BC, writing, “I came, I saw, I conquered.”

beats.scene: A smiling ruler in a laurel wreath pardons a kneeling man in the Forum
beats.summary: As dictator Caesar pardons his enemies, raises the poor, and reforms the calendar with the help of Egyptian astronomers.

beats.scene: A man offers a golden crown to a seated ruler as crowds watch
beats.summary: At a festival in 44 BC Mark Antony offers Caesar a king's crown three times, and Caesar refuses it, but many Romans suspect him.

beats.scene: A thoughtful man reads a note left on a judge's chair
beats.summary: Cassius and others plan to kill Caesar, and notes saying “You are sleeping, Brutus” persuade Brutus to join.

beats.scene: A frightened woman holds a man's sleeve in a shadowy bedroom
beats.summary: On the night before the Ides of March, Calpurnia dreams of Caesar's death, and Caesar wonders which death is best.

beats.scene: A fortune-teller stands by the road facing a man in a litter
beats.summary: A soothsayer had warned Caesar to beware the Ides of March, and on the day itself Caesar says they have come.

beats.scene: Senators in white togas crowd around a seated man beside a statue
beats.summary: In the Senate on the Ides of March 44 BC the conspirators crowd around Caesar and stab him, and he falls at the foot of Pompey's statue.

beats.scene: A crowd in the Forum watches a bloodstained toga raised on a pole
beats.summary: At Caesar's funeral Antony stirs the crowd to anger, and the killers flee from Rome.

beats.scene: A tall ghost stands in a dark tent before a startled commander
beats.summary: Brutus sees a ghost who says it will meet him at Philippi, and in 42 BC he loses the battle there and takes his own life.

beats.scene: A schoolboy in a toga reads a scroll while older men watch him
beats.summary: Cicero is born in 106 BC in Arpinum, gets an odd family name from a chickpea-shaped mark on a forefather's nose, and shines at school.

beats.scene: A thin young man practises speaking to an empty hall
beats.summary: Cicero has a weak voice, studies law and rhetoric in Rome, Athens and Rhodes, and trains his voice until it is strong.

beats.scene: A Roman lawyer holds up account books before a nervous governor
beats.summary: As quaestor in Sicily he governs honestly, and in 70 BC he prosecutes the corrupt governor Verres and wins.

beats.scene: A consul in a white toga points at a man in a crowded hall
beats.summary: As consul in 63 BC Cicero learns that Catiline plans a revolt, and he confronts Catiline in the Senate.

beats.scene: Foreign envoys hand a bundle of sealed letters to a consul
beats.summary: Catiline flees to the army he has raised, and Cicero catches the plotters inside Rome with letters carried by foreign envoys.

beats.scene: Senators in a lamplit hall stand on two sides of a bench
beats.summary: The Senate debates the fate of the five, and Caesar argues for prison while Cato demands death.

beats.scene: A weary man in a cloak looks back at a city on a hill
beats.summary: Cicero's enemy Clodius has him exiled in 58 BC, and he mourns in a foreign land, but a year later is welcomed home.

beats.scene: A father stands alone at his desk beside an empty chair
beats.summary: Cicero sides with Pompey in the civil war, is forgiven by Caesar, and grieves for his daughter Tullia in 45 BC.

beats.scene: A speaker raises his arm toward a crowded Senate while a soldier glares
beats.summary: After Caesar's death Cicero attacks Antony in speeches called the Philippics, but Antony, Octavian and Lepidus join forces and list their enemies.

beats.scene: Soldiers stop a litter on a country road at evening
beats.summary: Cicero is killed by Antony's soldiers in December 43 BC, and his head and hands are shown in the Forum.

beats.scene: A Roman general sits on a platform in a market square beside a river
beats.summary: After Philippi Mark Antony rules the East and summons Cleopatra to Tarsus in 41 BC to answer for helping his enemies.

beats.scene: A golden barge with purple sails drifts up a river past a crowd
beats.summary: Cleopatra sails up the river Cydnus on a golden barge, dressed as the goddess of love, and Antony is left alone in the market place.

beats.scene: A queen in a bright room speaks with ambassadors from many lands
beats.summary: Cleopatra's beauty is not her greatest power, as her voice and talk are charming, and she speaks many languages.

beats.scene: A queen laughs as a man hauls up a fish on a line
beats.summary: In Alexandria Antony forgets his duties among feasts and games, and Cleopatra teases him by having a salted fish hung on his line.

beats.scene: A thin, tired army crosses a bare mountain pass in the snow
beats.summary: Antony marries Octavian's sister Octavia for peace, then loses many men in a failed campaign against Parthia and returns to Cleopatra.

beats.scene: A man in a toga reads a document aloud to a restless crowd
beats.summary: Octavian reads Antony's will in Rome, which wants Antony buried in Egypt, and turns the Romans against him, and war is declared on Cleopatra.

beats.scene: Warships clash at sea while a few ships turn away and flee
beats.summary: At the sea battle of Actium in 31 BC, Cleopatra's ships turn and flee, and Antony abandons his fleet to follow her.

beats.scene: A queen watches from a tall tomb window as men lift a wounded soldier
beats.summary: In 30 BC, with Octavian at the gates of Alexandria, Antony hears a false report of Cleopatra's death, wounds himself and dies in her arms.

beats.scene: A queen in royal robes sits quietly beside a basket of figs
beats.summary: Cleopatra is captured by Octavian and dies soon after, by poison in a way that nobody knows for sure, and Egypt becomes a Roman province.

beats.scene: An old Greek priest in a temple at Delphi writes by lamplight
beats.summary: Plutarch pairs his Greeks and Romans to compare their virtues and faults, and his Lives shape later writers, including Shakespeare.

A1A2: Plutarch wrote about famous lives because small things show what a person is like.
Plutarch was born about the year 46 in a small Greek town.
As a young man, he went to Athens to study with a famous teacher.
Greece belonged to Rome then, and Plutarch visited the great city.
Later he became a priest at Delphi, the temple of Apollo.
He wrote about a Greek and a Roman, and compared the two.
Plutarch said a good painter looks closely at a man's face.
A small joke, he said, can tell more than a great battle.
He tells old stories, but he warns that some may not be true.
He hoped readers would learn to live well from these lives.
Theseus grew up in Troezen with his mother and his grandfather.
The boys ran from a lion skin, but Theseus fetched an axe.
At sixteen, Theseus lifted a heavy rock and found a sword.
His mother wanted him to go by sea, but he chose the road.
The first robber had a huge club, but Theseus beat him.
Sinis bent pine trees, and Theseus beat him with his own trick.
Theseus killed a huge wild pig and then stopped the robber Sciron.
At last he beat Procrustes, who made every traveller fit his bed.
At last Theseus reached Athens, but he told no one his name.
The king saw his own sword and knocked the cup away.
Theseus caught a wild bull at Marathon and led it to Athens.
In those days Athens had to send young people to King Minos.
Theseus promised his father to fly a white sail if he lived.
In Crete, the king's daughter Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread.
Theseus followed the thread into the maze and killed the monster.
Theseus and the young people escaped from Crete in a ship.
On Delos, they danced a winding dance to thank the gods.
Theseus forgot the white sail, and his father saw only black.
King Theseus brought many small villages together into one city, Athens.
Centuries later, Athens brought his bones home and built a shrine.
A wicked king took the throne of Alba from his brother.
The cruel king sent the twin babies down the river.
A she-wolf fed the twins until a shepherd found them.
The twins grew strong and led the young shepherds.
The twins learned the truth and gave the throne to Numitor.
The brothers watched the sky to decide who would rule.
Remus jumped over the new wall, and Romulus lost his brother.
Rome was full of men, but there were almost no women.
The women ran between the armies and stopped the fighting.
Romulus vanished in a storm, and the Romans honoured him as a god.
Lycurgus showed the Spartans their new king, his baby nephew.
Lycurgus travelled to other lands to study their laws.
The Spartans asked him to come home and lead them.
He made a council of old men to help rule Sparta.
He divided the land so every Spartan family had an equal share.
A young man hurt Lycurgus, but Lycurgus answered him with kindness.
Sparta used heavy iron money, so nobody wanted to steal it.
Every Spartan man ate his meals with the others at long tables.
Spartan boys learned to bear cold, hunger and pain without complaining.
He made the Spartans promise to keep his laws until he returned.
Solon was a poet and a trader who loved to learn.
Solon pretended to be mad and moved Athens with a poem.
Many poor farmers owed money, and some lost their freedom.
Solon cancelled the debts, and the poor were free again.
Solon brought home Athenians who had been sold as slaves.
Solon gave even the poorest men a vote in the assembly.
Solon wrote his laws on wooden tablets for all to read.
Then Solon sailed away for ten years and visited Egypt.
In rich Lydia, Solon told King Croesus that happiness may not last.
Peisistratus tricked the Athenians and took power, and Solon grew sad.
Aristides was poor, but everyone trusted him to be fair.
A farmer who could not write asked Aristides to write for him.
Themistocles taught Athens to build ships to fight the Persians.
Delphi told Athens to trust its wooden wall, meaning ships.
Themistocles told the Spartan, “Strike me, but listen to me.”
At night, Aristides brought news that Persian ships had surrounded the Greeks.
The Greeks won at Salamis, and the Persian king went home.
Aristides died poor, and Athens paid for his daughters' weddings.
After the war, Athens turned against Themistocles and sent him away.
The Persian king welcomed Themistocles and gave him a home.
Pericles was a calm man with a long head.
Pericles learned to think about nature from the wise Anaxagoras.
Pericles stayed away from parties and walked only to his work.
Pericles paid citizens to serve on juries, so poor men could serve.
Pericles built the Parthenon on the hill, and many people worked.
The sculptor Pheidias made a great statue, but enemies accused him.
Pericles loved Aspasia, a clever woman, and kissed her every day.
War began with Sparta, and a plague struck crowded Athens.
Pericles lost his sons, but the people chose him again.
As he died, Pericles said no Athenian had worn mourning because of him.
Alcibiades lay in the road so a cart had to stop.
He refused to learn the flute because it twisted his face.
Socrates talked to Alcibiades, and sometimes the young man cried.
Alcibiades cut the tail off his fine dog on purpose.
In battle Socrates saved the life of Alcibiades.
Alcibiades persuaded Athens to send a great fleet to Sicily.
One night, the stone statues were broken, and people blamed Alcibiades.
In Sparta, Alcibiades ate black broth and lived like a Spartan.
In 407 BC, Alcibiades came home to Athens as a hero.
Alcibiades lost the trust of Athens again and died far away.
Demosthenes lost his father young, and his guardians took his money.
The crowd laughed at his first speech, and he felt ashamed.
He talked with stones in his mouth and shouted at the sea.
He studied underground for months, so he shaved half his head.
Demosthenes warned Athens that King Philip of Macedon was dangerous.
At last Demosthenes made Athens and Thebes join against Philip.
Philip won at Chaeronea, and Greece lost its freedom.
Demosthenes told a story about sheep, dogs and hungry wolves.
After Alexander died, Athens fought again, but Demosthenes had to flee.
Demosthenes took poison in a temple rather than be caught.
Alexander was born in Macedon, the son of King Philip.
Each time Philip won a victory, young Alexander worried.
Alexander calmed the wild black horse by turning it toward the sun.
Aristotle taught the young prince, who loved books and Homer.
The boy Alexander asked the Persian visitors a lot of questions.
At eighteen, Alexander led the horsemen at the battle of Chaeronea.
At the wedding feast, Alexander threw his cup at Attalus.
Philip was killed in 336 BC, and Alexander became king.
Alexander destroyed Thebes but spared the house of Pindar.
Diogenes lay in the sun and asked Alexander to step aside.
Alexander gave his lands to his friends and kept only hope.
At Troy, Alexander honoured Achilles and said he envied him.
Alexander crossed the Granicus river and fought the Persian army.
At Gordium, Alexander cut the famous knot with his sword.
Alexander beat Darius and treated his family with kindness.
Alexander built a road across the sea to reach the city of Tyre.
Alexander planned a new city by the sea and named it Alexandria.
Alexander crossed the desert to ask a god a question.
Alexander slept soundly before the big battle with Darius.
At Persepolis, a drunken feast ended with the palace on fire.
Alexander refused water when his soldiers were all thirsty.
Darius was killed by his own men, and Alexander wept.
Alexander killed his friend Cleitus in anger, and then wept.
Alexander defeated the Indian king Porus but treated him as a king.
Old Bucephalus died, and Alexander built a city for him.
The tired soldiers refused to go farther, so Alexander turned back.
On the long journey home, an arrow struck Alexander in battle.
In the hot desert, many of Alexander's tired soldiers died.
Greeks and Persians married each other, but then Hephaestion died.
Alexander died in Babylon and left his kingdom to the strongest.
Marcius was raised by his mother Volumnia, and he became a brave soldier.
The poor people left Rome, but a wise man called them back.
Marcius rushed into the enemy city, and the Romans followed him.
The general gave Marcius a new name, Coriolanus, for his courage.
Coriolanus wanted to be consul, but the voters said no.
There was no bread, and the poor people were angry.
The people sent Coriolanus away, and he left Rome sadly.
Coriolanus went to Rome's enemy, the Volscian leader Aufidius.
Coriolanus led the Volscian army to Rome, and the people were afraid.
His mother begged him, and Coriolanus took his army home.
Pyrrhus planned to fight Rome, but his wise friend asked a question.
The Romans had never seen elephants, and Pyrrhus won the battle.
A Roman named Fabricius refused the king's gold and was not afraid.
Pyrrhus won again, but he said another win would ruin him.
As a boy, Fabius was so gentle that people called him the Lamb.
Fabius followed Hannibal but would not fight him, and people laughed.
Hannibal escaped at night by tying burning torches to many cattle.
Minucius led his own army and got into danger, so Fabius helped him.
The Romans fought Hannibal in a big battle and lost badly.
Fabius lived to be an old man, and Rome honoured him.
Cato worked on his own farm and ate the same food as his workers.
As a young man, Cato fought in the war against Hannibal.
A rich neighbour told Cato to go to Rome and speak.
Cato became consul and led the army in Spain.
Cato led soldiers over the mountain and surprised the enemy king.
As censor, Cato punished rich men who lived with too much luxury.
Cato did not trust the clever Greek teachers who visited Rome.
Cato showed the senators fresh figs from Carthage, which was close.
Cato ended every speech by saying that Carthage must be destroyed.
Cato died in 149 BC, and Rome destroyed Carthage soon afterwards.
Pirates captured young Caesar, but he laughed at their small price.
Caesar stayed with the pirates for weeks and acted like their master.
After he was freed, Caesar caught the pirates and kept his promise.
Caesar read about Alexander and cried about his own life.
Caesar joined two powerful men, Pompey and Crassus, and became consul.
Caesar spent years at war in a far country, and his soldiers loved him.
Two deaths broke the alliance, and Pompey became Caesar's enemy.
Caesar crossed the little river Rubicon and began a civil war.
Caesar won a great battle at Pharsalus, and Pompey ran away.
Pompey was killed in Egypt, and Caesar wept when he heard.
Cleopatra had a servant carry her to Caesar in a bag.
Caesar won more wars and wrote, “I came, I saw, I won.”
Caesar ruled Rome and was kind to his old enemies.
At a festival, Antony offered Caesar a crown, but Caesar refused.
Many men planned to kill Caesar, and Brutus joined them.
Calpurnia had a bad dream and begged Caesar to stay home.
Caesar was told, “Be careful on the Ides of March,” but he went.
Caesar's enemies attacked him in the Senate, and he fell down.
Antony's speech made the crowd angry, and the killers left Rome.
At Philippi, Brutus lost the battle and ended his own life.
Cicero was a clever boy from a small town in Italy.
Cicero's voice was weak, so he worked hard to make it strong.
Cicero spoke against a corrupt governor named Verres, and he won.
As consul, Cicero learned that Catiline planned to attack Rome.
Catiline left Rome, and Cicero arrested his friends who stayed.
The senators argued about what to do with the five men.
Cicero's enemies sent him away, but Rome later called him home.
Cicero lost his daughter Tullia, and he wrote books to forget his grief.
Cicero spoke against Antony, but then the leaders joined together against him.
Cicero was killed by Antony's soldiers in 43 BC.
Antony ruled the East and called Queen Cleopatra to meet him.
Cleopatra sailed up the river in a golden boat with purple sails.
Cleopatra was charming, and she could speak many languages.
In Egypt, Antony enjoyed feasts and games with Cleopatra.
Antony lost many men in a war, and then returned to Cleopatra.
Octavian read Antony's will, and the Romans grew angry with him.
At Actium, Cleopatra's ships fled, and Antony sailed after her.
Antony heard a false story about Cleopatra's death and wounded himself.
Cleopatra died soon after Antony, and Egypt became part of Rome.
Plutarch's books lived on, and Shakespeare used them for his plays.
B1B2: Plutarch, a Greek priest of Delphi, explains that he is not writing history but lives. A small joke or a simple act, he says, often shows a person's character better than a great battle.
Plutarch was born about AD 46 in Chaeronea, a small town in the hills of Greece. He stayed there for most of his life, because he said he did not want the little town to grow even smaller.

When he was a young man, Plutarch went to Athens to study philosophy under a teacher named Ammonius. There he learned to ask questions, to weigh both sides of an argument and to love the great writers of the past.
In his time Greece was part of the Roman empire, and its great days were long over. Plutarch visited Rome, gave talks there and made friends among powerful Romans.

Plutarch became a priest of Apollo at Delphi, where visitors came from far away to ask the god about their future. He served there for many years and wrote about the temple's customs and its old stories.

Plutarch's great plan was to write the lives of famous men in pairs, one Greek and one Roman. He chose men whose lives looked alike, so that the reader could compare their courage, their mistakes and their ends.

Plutarch compared himself to a painter who studies the face and the eyes, because these show the soul. He left the great battles to other writers and looked instead for the signs of a man's character.
A short saying, a small joke or a kind act, Plutarch writes, often shows more of a man than a battle with thousands of dead. That is why his pages are full of little stories.

Plutarch says that mapmakers crowd the edges of their maps with deserts and wild beasts, because they know nothing more. Very early history is like that, and he promises to say clearly when a story is only a legend.
Plutarch says that he began writing lives for the sake of others, but he soon found that he was learning too. For him each great life was a mirror in which he could correct his own habits.
Theseus was born in the small city of Troezen, where his mother Aethra and his grandfather Pittheus brought him up. His father Aegeus was king of Athens, but he lived far away across the water.
When the great Hercules visited Troezen, he took off his lion skin and left it on a chair. The boys ran away in fear, but young Theseus took an axe, believing that the lion was alive.
When Theseus was sixteen, his mother led him to a huge rock and told him the secret. He lifted it easily and took out the sword and sandals that Aegeus had hidden there.

His grandfather and his mother begged him to go to Athens by sea, because the road was full of robbers. Theseus refused, because he wanted to follow the example of Hercules and make the roads safe for travellers.
The first robber he met was Periphetes, who killed travellers with an iron club. Theseus defeated him and kept the club for himself, to remind him of his victory.
At the Isthmus lived Sinis, who bent two pine trees down and tied travellers between them. Theseus caught him and gave him the same punishment that he had given to so many others.
Theseus killed the great wild sow of Crommyon, which had terrified the farmers. Then he met Sciron, who threw travellers from a high cliff into the sea, and he threw Sciron into the sea himself.

At Eleusis, Theseus beat Cercyon, who wrestled strangers to the death, by using skill rather than strength. Then he met Procrustes, whose iron bed was meant to fit every traveller exactly, and he gave him the same treatment he had given them.

After washing away the guilt of his killings at the river Cephisus, Theseus entered Athens. The city was full of quarrels, and old King Aegeus lived under the spell of Medea, his wife, who feared a rival to her son.
Medea persuaded the king to give the stranger a cup of poison at dinner. But when Theseus drew his sword to cut the meat, Aegeus recognised it and knocked the cup from his hand.
Some of the king's own nephews wanted the throne for themselves, but Theseus defeated their plot. Then he caught the wild bull that was terrifying the farmers at Marathon and led it through Athens.

Long before, the son of King Minos had been killed in Athenian lands, and Minos had made the Athenians pay a terrible price. Every nine years they had to send seven boys and seven girls to Crete, and none ever came home.
The ship that carried the young people always sailed with a black sail, as a sign of mourning. Aegeus gave his son a white sail and begged him to raise it on the way home, if he was alive.
In Crete, Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, fell in love with Theseus the moment she saw him. She gave him a ball of thread and told him how to find his way out of the maze.

Theseus entered the Labyrinth with the thread in his hand, and he followed the twisting paths into the darkness. In the heart of the maze he found the Minotaur, half man and half bull, and he killed it.

That night Theseus and the young Athenians slipped out of the harbour and sailed away, taking Ariadne with them. Writers tell different stories about her, and Plutarch admits that no one agrees about what became of her.
On their way home they stopped at the island of Delos, to thank Apollo and to leave an offering. There Theseus led the young people in a dance whose winding steps copied the paths of the Labyrinth.
In the joy of the victory, Theseus forgot to change the black sail for the white one. Aegeus, watching from a high rock, believed his son was dead and threw himself into the sea.

As king, Theseus brought the scattered villages of Attica together into one city, Athens. He gave the people a voice, kept the command of the army for himself and held a great festival to celebrate the union.

In his later years the Athenians turned against Theseus, and he died far from home on the island of Scyros. About 475 BC, the general Cimon found his bones there and brought them to Athens, where a shrine was built.

In the old city of Alba Longa, a king named Amulius pushed his brother Numitor from the throne. He made Numitor's daughter Rhea Silvia a priestess who could never marry, but she gave birth to twin boys.
Amulius ordered a servant to put the baby boys in a trough and leave them to the river Tiber. The river was in flood, so the trough drifted gently to the shore at the foot of a hill.
A she-wolf came down to the river and fed the babies with her milk, while a woodpecker brought them scraps of food. Then a shepherd named Faustulus found them and took them home to his wife.
The twins grew into strong, brave young men, and the other shepherds followed them. One day they quarrelled with the herdsmen of Numitor, and Remus was captured and taken before the old king.
Faustulus finally told the brothers the truth about their birth, and Numitor learned who they were. Together they killed the wicked Amulius and gave the throne back to their grandfather.
They agreed to settle the matter by watching for birds. Remus saw six vultures first, but Romulus soon saw twelve, and each brother claimed the victory.

Romulus marked out his city with a plough and began to build a low wall. Remus laughed at it and jumped over it, and in the quarrel that followed he was killed, though stories differ about who struck him.

To fill his new city, Romulus offered a safe home to anyone in trouble, and many men came. But Rome had almost no women, so at a festival the Romans carried off the daughters of their Sabine neighbours.

The Sabine king Titus Tatius marched against Rome to win back the women, and after many battles the two armies faced each other. Then the women ran between them, begging their fathers and their husbands to stop, and peace was made.

Romulus reigned for many years, but one day, while he was inspecting his army, a sudden storm covered the field with darkness. When the light returned, the king had vanished, and a Roman named Proculus swore that he had seen Romulus rise to heaven.

Lycurgus was the brother of a king of Sparta, and when the king died, the throne might have been his. Instead he lifted his tiny nephew in his arms and told the Spartans that a king had been born to them.
To escape the quarrels at home, Lycurgus travelled to Crete and to Asia, where he studied the laws and customs of many peoples. He also copied out the poems of Homer and brought them back to Greece.

Back in Sparta, the kings and the people were quarrelling, and they begged Lycurgus to return. Before changing anything he went to Delphi, where the priestess called him dear to the gods and promised that his laws would be the best.

Lycurgus created a council of twenty-eight elders, who sat with the two kings and checked their power. The people also met in an assembly, where they could say yes or no to proposals but could not argue about them.
Lycurgus saw that a few Spartans had huge estates while many had no land at all. He divided the land into equal lots, so that every citizen had enough to live on and nobody was very rich.

Some rich Spartans hated the new laws, and a young man named Alcander hit Lycurgus with a stick and blinded one eye. The people gave Alcander to Lycurgus to punish, but Lycurgus took him into his house and taught him patience and kindness.

Lycurgus banned gold and silver coins and made Sparta's money from iron, soaked in vinegar so that it became brittle. A small sum took a cart and a pair of oxen to carry, so stealing and hoarding became almost useless.
Lycurgus made all the men eat together in groups of about fifteen, at plain tables, instead of at home. The most famous dish was black broth, which other Greeks said tasted terrible.

At the age of seven, Spartan boys left home to be trained together, with little food and a thin cloak. Plutarch tells of a boy who hid a stolen fox under his cloak and kept silent, even though it hurt him badly.

When his laws were ready, Lycurgus made the kings and the citizens swear to keep them until he came back. Then he went to Delphi, where the god approved his laws, and he chose never to return, so that the oath would last forever.

Solon came from a good Athenian family, but his father had spent most of its money, so he worked as a merchant and travelled widely. He wrote poems all his life, and he said that he grew old always learning something new.

Athens had lost the island of Salamis to its neighbour Megara, and it was a crime even to speak of taking it back. Solon pretended to be mad, ran into the market in a felt cap and recited a poem that woke the people's courage.
In Athens the poor farmers borrowed from the rich, and if they could not pay, they lost their land. Some were even sold as slaves, and the city came close to a civil war.

In about 594 BC the Athenians chose Solon to settle their quarrels, because the poor trusted him and the rich respected him. His first act was to cancel the debts that were crushing the poor, a reform called the shaking-off of burdens.

Solon also freed the Athenians who had become slaves because of their debts. He brought back many who had been sold abroad, some of whom had been away so long that they had forgotten their own language.
Solon divided the Athenians into four groups by their wealth. The richest could hold the highest offices, but even the poorest men had a vote in the assembly and could help judge cases in court.
Solon wrote the new laws on wooden tablets and set them up where everyone could read them. He even made a law that a citizen who refused to take either side in a civil quarrel would lose his rights.
People kept coming to Solon to ask him to explain or change the laws, and he grew tired of it. He said he was going on a trading journey, and he sailed away for ten years, visiting Egypt and Cyprus.

In Lydia Solon met King Croesus, who was proud of his huge treasure and expected Solon to call him the happiest of men. Solon replied that nobody can be called happy until his life is over, because fortune can change at any time.

Back in Athens, Solon saw his relative Peisistratus wound himself and ride into the market, claiming that enemies had attacked him. The people gave him bodyguards, and with them he made himself the ruler of Athens, although he kept most of Solon's laws.

Aristides was an Athenian who earned the name of the Just, because he would never take a bribe or favour a friend. When the Persians landed at Marathon in 490 BC, he gave up his turn to command the army so that Miltiades could lead it alone.

The Athenians could vote to exile a powerful man for ten years by writing his name on a broken piece of pottery. A farmer who could not write asked Aristides himself to scratch the name Aristides, saying he was tired of hearing him called the Just.

The victory at Marathon would not let the young Themistocles sleep, because he knew that the Persians would return. He persuaded the Athenians to spend the silver from their mines on a fleet, saying that ships alone could save the city.

In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes marched against Greece with a huge army. The priestess at Delphi told the Athenians to trust a wooden wall, and Themistocles explained that she meant ships, so the people left the city.

The Greek commanders wanted to sail away from Salamis, and they argued bitterly in the council. When the Spartan commander Eurybiades raised his stick to stop Themistocles speaking, Themistocles said, “Strike me, but listen to me.”

Themistocles secretly sent a servant to tell Xerxes that the Greeks were about to run away, and the Persian ships moved to block every exit. That night Aristides, the exile, slipped through them to tell Themistocles that the Greeks were surrounded, and the old rivals joined forces.

At dawn the huge Persian fleet pushed into the narrow strait, where the ships were so crowded that they got in each other's way. The Greeks, fighting close to home, won a great victory in 480 BC, while Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore.

Aristides later led the Athenians at the great victory of Plataea in 479 BC, and he set fair payments for the allies of Athens. Although he had handled huge sums, he died so poor that the city paid for his funeral and his daughters' weddings.

After the war the Greeks honoured Themistocles so much that at the Olympic Games the crowd turned from the races to look at him. But the Athenians grew jealous of his fame, and they sent him into exile.

Themistocles escaped to Persia and, after learning to speak Persian, he was welcomed by King Artaxerxes, who gave him three cities to rule. He lived there in comfort until his death around 460 BC, and some said that he took poison rather than fight against Athens.

Pericles came from a noble family, and he had a long, oddly shaped head, so statues show him in a helmet. He was famous for his calm voice and his serious manner, and he never lost his temper in public.

Pericles studied with the philosopher Anaxagoras, who taught him to look for natural causes instead of fearing signs and wonders. When a ram with one horn was brought to him, the seer Lampon called it an omen, but Anaxagoras explained its strange skull.
Pericles rarely went to dinners or parties, and he was seen only on the road to the market and the council house. In this way he kept his dignity, and people trusted him to be honest.

Pericles introduced pay for those who served on juries, so that a poor man could take part in the government without losing a day's wages. Critics said that he was buying the people's love, but his supporters said he was making Athens fairer.

Pericles used the wealth of Athens to build the Parthenon and other temples on the Acropolis. Thousands of stone-cutters, carpenters and sculptors found work, and the buildings were finished with astonishing speed.

The sculptor Pheidias directed the works and made a giant statue of Athena in gold and ivory. His enemies, who wanted to hurt Pericles, accused him of stealing gold, but the gold was weighed and none was missing.

In private life Pericles loved a clever woman named Aspasia, who came from the city of Miletus. Plutarch says that he kissed her every morning when he left for the market, and that Socrates went to hear her talk.

When war with Sparta began in 431 BC, Pericles told the farmers to move inside the walls of Athens and rely on the fleet. The city became crowded, and in the second summer a terrible plague broke out.
The plague killed many of Pericles's friends and both of his legitimate sons. At the funeral of the younger one, Paralus, he tried to stay calm, but as he laid the wreath on the body, he wept.

In 429 BC, Pericles fell ill with the plague, and as he lay dying his friends spoke softly about his great deeds. He surprised them by saying that his finest honour was that no Athenian had ever put on mourning because of him.

Alcibiades was handsome, clever and rich, and after his father's death he was raised by Pericles. As a boy he was playing dice when a cart came, and he lay down in front of it until the driver stopped.

When a stronger boy had him pinned in a wrestling match, Alcibiades bit his arm, and the boy said that he bit like a woman. Alcibiades replied that he bit like a lion, and later he refused to learn the flute, because playing it twisted the face.
Many people admired the handsome Alcibiades, and most of them flattered him. Only the philosopher Socrates could make him blush and weep, by showing him how little he knew about being good.

Alcibiades owned a beautiful and very expensive dog, and one day he cut off its tail. When his friends were shocked, he said that he wanted the Athenians to talk about this, so that they would not talk about worse things.

In the war at Potidaea, Socrates and Alcibiades fought side by side, and Socrates saved the wounded young man. Years later, when the Athenians fled from the battle at Delium, Alcibiades rode beside Socrates to protect him.

In 415 BC Alcibiades argued that Athens should conquer Sicily, but the careful Nicias warned that it was too far and too dangerous. The Athenians, dazzled by the dream of a bigger empire, voted for the expedition, and a great fleet sailed.

One night the stone statues of the god Hermes were broken all over Athens, and enemies accused Alcibiades of the crime. Once in Sicily, he was ordered home for trial, but he escaped on the way and was sentenced to death in his absence.

In Sparta, Alcibiades cut his hair short, bathed in cold water and ate the black broth, so that everyone thought he was a true Spartan. He also advised the Spartans how to hurt Athens, which was very bitter for his native city.

After winning several battles at sea, Alcibiades returned to Athens in 407 BC, and the crowd cheered him as if he were a god. The people chose him as the leading general and forgave the old charges against him.

When his helmsman Antiochus, left in command, lost a battle at Notium, the Athenians blamed Alcibiades and removed him. He fled to Phrygia, where assassins surrounded his house in 404 BC, set fire to it and killed him as he rushed out.

Demosthenes was only seven when his rich father died, and the men who looked after his money cheated him. When he grew up, he studied speaking and took them to court, though he got back little of what he had lost.
Demosthenes had a weak voice, and the crowd laughed at his first speech in the assembly. He went home in despair, but the actor Satyrus showed him how much a good delivery matters.

Demosthenes practised speaking with pebbles in his mouth to cure his stammer, and he recited verses while running uphill to strengthen his breath. On the beach he shouted against the roar of the waves, so that he would not be afraid of a noisy crowd.

Demosthenes built a small room underground, where he studied and practised for months at a time. To stop himself going out, he shaved half of his head, because he was too ashamed to be seen in public.

King Philip of Macedon was growing stronger every year and taking cities in northern Greece. Demosthenes warned the Athenians again and again that Philip wanted to rule all Greece, but many of them did not want to hear it.

When Philip marched south, Demosthenes hurried to Thebes, which had long been an enemy of Athens. By his powerful speeches he persuaded the Thebans to join the Athenians, and the two cities faced Philip together.

In 338 BC Philip and his young son Alexander defeated the Greek armies at Chaeronea, which was Plutarch's own town. After the battle, Demosthenes was accused of running away, though he went on serving Athens.

When Alexander became king, he demanded that Athens hand over ten of its leading speakers, including Demosthenes. Demosthenes told the crowd a fable in which wolves asked the sheep to give up their dogs, and the Athenians saw the danger.

When Alexander died in 323 BC, Demosthenes urged the Athenians to rebel against Macedon, but the revolt failed. Antipater, the Macedonian general, demanded the speakers, and Demosthenes escaped by sea.

On the island of Calauria, Demosthenes took refuge in the temple of Poseidon, but the agent Archias came to take him. Asking for time to write a letter, he put his pen to his lips, swallowed the poison hidden in it and died in 322 BC.
Alexander was born in 356 BC, the son of King Philip of Macedon and Queen Olympias. His father's family said that they came from Hercules, and his mother's family said that they came from Achilles.
As a boy Alexander was quick, strong and a fast runner. Each time news came that Philip had won a city, he told his friends that his father would leave nothing great for him to do.
A dealer brought a magnificent black horse to Philip, but no one could ride it. Alexander saw that the horse feared its own shadow, so he turned it toward the sun, calmed it and rode it.
Philip invited the great thinker Aristotle to teach his son in a quiet garden at Mieza. Alexander loved learning, and he kept a copy of Homer's Iliad under his pillow, next to his dagger.
When Philip was away, Persian envoys came to his court, and the young Alexander received them. He did not ask about gold or palaces, but about the roads, the army and the character of their king.

At the age of eighteen, Alexander led the Macedonian cavalry in the battle at Chaeronea. His horsemen were said to be the first to break the Sacred Band of Thebes, the most famous fighting unit in Greece.
When Philip married a new wife, her uncle Attalus said at the feast that Philip would now have a true heir. Alexander threw his cup at him, and the angry Philip drew his sword but fell down drunk.
In 336 BC a young bodyguard named Pausanias killed Philip at a wedding festival. Alexander, who was only twenty, became king and found himself surrounded by enemies at home and abroad.

In 335 BC the city of Thebes rebelled, and Alexander took it by storm and destroyed it as a warning to the other Greeks. He spared the temples and the house of the poet Pindar, who had died more than a century before.

At Corinth the Greek cities chose Alexander as their leader against Persia, and many famous men came to praise him. Only Diogenes stayed away, so Alexander visited him and asked what he wanted, and Diogenes said, “Stand out of my sun.”
