In 334 BC Alexander crossed into Asia with a modest army and little money. He gave away most of his lands to his friends, and when Perdiccas asked what he had kept for himself, he said, “Hope.”

At Troy, Alexander placed a wreath on the tomb of Achilles and ran around it with his friends. He said that Achilles was fortunate to have had a faithful friend and a great poet like Homer to praise him.

At the river Granicus in 334 BC, Alexander led his horsemen across the water and attacked the Persian army on the far bank. In the fighting a Persian nobleman raised his axe to strike him, but his friend Cleitus struck first and saved his life.
In the city of Gordium stood an old cart tied with a knot that nobody could undo. A legend said that the man who loosened it would rule Asia, so Alexander drew his sword and cut through it.

In 333 BC Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius at Issus, and Darius fled, leaving his mother, wife and daughters behind. Alexander treated them with great respect and told them that Darius was still alive.
In 332 BC the island city of Tyre refused to open its gates to Alexander. He built a long stone causeway across the sea, and after many months of siege the city fell.
In Egypt, Alexander chose a site by the sea for a new city, and he named it Alexandria. The builders had no chalk, so they marked its outline with barley meal, and the birds came down and ate it.

Alexander crossed the desert to a temple of the god Ammon, where the priest greeted him as the god's son. Later he said that Zeus is the father of all men, but that he makes the best of them especially his own.

On the morning of the battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC, Alexander was still asleep when his generals came to him. Parmenio had to wake him, and the king explained that he slept well because the long chase was nearly over.

After taking Babylon and Susa, Alexander reached Persepolis, the Persian capital, where he found huge treasures. At a drunken feast one night, the guests set the palace on fire, and Alexander soon regretted it.

While chasing Darius across a hot desert, Alexander was almost mad with thirst. Some soldiers brought him water in a helmet, but he saw his men watching and handed it back, saying he would not drink alone.
Darius's own officers, led by Bessus, arrested him and then left him dying in a cart. When Alexander arrived, he took off his own cloak, covered the body and ordered a royal funeral.

At a drunken feast in 328 BC, Cleitus praised Philip above Alexander and boasted that his own hand had saved the king at Granicus. Alexander snatched a spear and killed him, and afterwards he lay for three days in tears.

In 326 BC Alexander crossed the river Hydaspes in a storm and defeated King Porus, who fought bravely with his elephants. Alexander asked how he wanted to be treated, and Porus answered, “Like a king.”
The faithful Bucephalus, who had carried Alexander for many years, died soon after the battle with Porus. Alexander mourned him like a friend and founded a city beside the river with his name.

After years of marching, Alexander's soldiers heard that great armies waited beyond the next river, and they refused to go on. Alexander sulked in his tent for days, but finally he agreed to turn back.

Alexander sailed down the rivers of India toward the sea, fighting local tribes along the way. In the town of the Malli an arrow pierced his armour and wounded him badly, but his friends carried him to safety and he recovered.
On the way back to Persia, Alexander chose to lead his army through the hot Gedrosian desert. The march was terrible, and many soldiers died of thirst and heat before the rest reached green land.

At Susa in 324 BC Alexander married a daughter of Darius and arranged marriages between his officers and Persian women. Not long afterwards his dearest friend Hephaestion died, and Alexander was overcome with grief.

In June 323 BC Alexander fell ill with a fever in Babylon, and his soldiers filed past his bed to say goodbye. He died at the age of thirty-two, and when his friends asked who should inherit, he is said to have answered, “The strongest.”
Gaius Marcius lost his father when he was very young, and his mother Volumnia raised him alone. He grew up brave and strong, but he was also proud and hard to please.

The poor of Rome were crushed by debt, so they left the city and camped on a hill outside it. An old senator named Menenius told them that the body's parts once rebelled against the belly, and that all of them became weak.
Rome was at war with the Volscians, and its army besieged their city of Corioli. Marcius charged through the gates with only a few men, fought his way inside, and the whole Roman army followed him.

After the battle the consul Cominius praised him before the whole army and gave him a fine horse. Marcius refused the treasure and asked only for the freedom of a poor man who had once been kind to him.

Roman custom said that a man who wanted office should show his scars to the voters and ask for their support. Coriolanus did this reluctantly, and the people, who disliked his proud manner, refused him the consulship.

A famine struck Rome, and shiploads of grain were sent for the hungry citizens. Coriolanus spoke against handing it out cheaply unless the people gave up their tribunes, and this made the poor furious.

The assembly voted to send Coriolanus into exile, and the crowd cheered in the streets. He said goodbye to his mother and his wife, who wept bitterly, and he walked out of Rome with only a few friends.

Coriolanus travelled to the Volscian city of Antium and sat down by the hearth in the house of Tullus Aufidius, his old enemy. He said that he would fight for the Volscians if Aufidius wished, or give up his life if not.

Soon a Volscian army under the command of Coriolanus and Aufidius reached the walls of Rome. The senate sent his old friends to beg for peace, and even priests in holy robes, but he sent them all away.

At last Volumnia, his wife and his children walked to the Volscian camp, and she spoke bitterly of what he was doing. Coriolanus rose, embraced her, and said, “Mother, you have saved Rome, but you have lost your son.”
Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, was invited by the Greek city of Tarentum to fight against Rome. His wise adviser Cineas asked what he would do after winning, and the king listed Italy, Sicily and Africa.

In 280 BC Pyrrhus landed in Italy with about twenty war elephants and met the Romans at Heraclea. The Romans and their horses had never seen such animals, and they were beaten, although Pyrrhus lost many of his best men.

Pyrrhus sent for the Roman envoy Fabricius and tried to give him gold, but the poor man refused. Next the king hid an elephant behind a curtain, but when it suddenly raised its trunk over him, Fabricius only smiled.
At Asculum in 279 BC Pyrrhus won a second battle, but his army had again lost far too many men. He said, “One more victory like this and we are lost,” and in time he sailed home.

Quintus Fabius Maximus had been a quiet, slow and gentle child, and his friends called him the Lamb. Years later, in 217 BC, Hannibal's armies had crushed the Roman legions in Italy, and Fabius was chosen to lead Rome.

Fabius decided not to meet Hannibal in open battle, because the Carthaginians were stronger on flat ground. He shadowed them on the hills and cut off their food, and the impatient Romans laughed at him for being afraid.

Fabius once closed the mountain passes and trapped Hannibal's army in a plain with no way out. That night Hannibal ordered about two thousand oxen to be driven up the hills with burning torches on their horns.

The impatient Romans gave Fabius's deputy Minucius the same power as the dictator, and Minucius soon rushed into a trap. Fabius marched out and rescued him, and Minucius came to him and called him “father.”
In 216 BC the Romans, who were tired of waiting, fought Hannibal at Cannae. About fifty thousand of them were killed, and the shocked Romans finally understood that Fabius had been wise.
When the Senate would not pay for prisoners taken by Hannibal, Fabius sold his own land to free them. He died as an old man in 203 BC, and every Roman gave a small coin to pay for his funeral.

Marcus Cato was born about 234 BC in the Italian countryside, and he worked his own small farm as a young man. He wore plain clothes, ate the same simple food as his workers, and drank the same cheap wine.

When Cato was still a young man, Rome was fighting for its life against Hannibal, and he joined the army. He marched on foot, carried his own gear, drank water and slept on the ground like the common soldiers.
A noble neighbour named Valerius Flaccus noticed Cato's sharp mind and urged him to go to Rome. There Cato spoke in the law courts for his friends, and his plain, forceful words soon made him famous.
In 195 BC the Romans elected Cato consul, and he was sent to Spain to put down a rebellion. He won several battles, took many towns, and came home to a triumph through the streets of Rome.
In 191 BC Cato served as an officer in a Roman war in Greece, against King Antiochus. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae he led soldiers over a mountain path and attacked the enemy from behind.

In 184 BC Cato was elected censor, an officer whose task was to judge the conduct of citizens. He removed one senator from the Senate, put heavy taxes on costly clothes and carriages, and made many enemies.

In 155 BC three Athenian philosophers came to Rome as envoys, and young Romans crowded to hear them argue. Cato feared that Greek talk would make Romans soft, and he urged the Senate to send the visitors home.

Once Cato was sent to Carthage to settle a quarrel, and he saw that the city had grown rich and strong again. Back home he dropped some fine figs from his toga in the Senate and said that they came from a land three days away.

After the visit Cato ended every speech in the Senate with the same sentence, whatever the subject was. “And besides, I think that Carthage must be destroyed,” he said, and Scipio Nasica answered that it should be left alone.
Cato lived to a great age and died in 149 BC, still writing books and sharp-tongued in the Senate. Three years later the Romans destroyed Carthage, exactly as he had wished.
While Julius Caesar was sailing to Rhodes to study, pirates captured his ship and demanded twenty talents of silver. He laughed at them for not knowing who he was, and told them to ask for fifty.

For about forty days Caesar lived among the pirates, and he behaved more like their commander than their prisoner. He joined their games, read them his poems and speeches, and told them to be quiet when he wanted to sleep.

When the money was paid, Caesar was set free, and he immediately gathered ships and men from the nearby cities. He caught most of the pirates, took back the silver, and punished them exactly as he had once promised.

Years later, in Spain, Caesar was reading about Alexander the Great, and he sat silent for a long time. He said that Alexander had ruled the world at his own age, while he had done nothing great at all.
Caesar could not rise alone, so he secretly joined Pompey, the great general, and Crassus, the richest man in Rome. In 59 BC he became consul, and afterwards he took command of the provinces of Gaul.

In about eight years of fighting, Caesar conquered Gaul, built a bridge across the Rhine, and crossed the sea to Britain. His soldiers loved him because he shared their hardships and rewarded their bravery.

Julia, Caesar's daughter and the wife of Pompey, died in 54 BC, and Crassus was killed in battle a year later. Without these links Pompey and Caesar became rivals, and the Senate ordered Caesar to give up his army.

In January 49 BC Caesar stood at the Rubicon, a small river that marked the edge of his province. He knew that to cross it with an army meant war, and at last he said, “Let the die be cast,” and went over.
In 48 BC the two armies met at Pharsalus in Greece, and Pompey had about twice as many men as Caesar. Caesar's tired veterans won the battle anyway, and Pompey fled from the field in despair.
Pompey sailed to Egypt hoping that the young king would help him, but the king's advisers had him killed as he landed. When Caesar arrived and saw Pompey's ring, he turned away and wept.

In Alexandria the young Queen Cleopatra was shut out of her palace by her brother's advisers. She had a servant roll her up in a bed-sack and carry her through the gates, and Caesar was amazed and charmed when she appeared.
After a hard war in Egypt, Caesar sailed to Asia and defeated King Pharnaces at the city of Zela in only a few days. He wrote to a friend, “I came, I saw, I conquered.”
After beating the last of his enemies, Caesar ruled Rome as dictator. He pardoned many of those who had fought against him, and he also reformed the calendar with the help of astronomers.
At a festival in 44 BC, Mark Antony tried three times to place a king's crown on Caesar's head. Each time Caesar pushed it away, but many Romans still thought that he secretly wanted to be king.

A group of senators led by Cassius began to plan Caesar's death, but they knew they needed Brutus, who was respected by all. Notes were left for him saying, “You are asleep, Brutus,” and he finally agreed to join them.

The night before, at a dinner, Caesar was asked which kind of death was best, and he said, “A sudden one.” That night his wife Calpurnia dreamed that she was holding his murdered body, and she begged him not to go out.
A soothsayer had warned Caesar to beware the Ides of March, and on that day he told the man, “The Ides of March have come.” “Yes,” said the old man, “but they have not gone.”

In the hall where the Senate was meeting, the plotters gathered around Caesar's chair as if to ask him a favour. When they drew their daggers he fought back, but when he saw Brutus he covered his face and fell at the foot of Pompey's statue.

At Caesar's funeral in the Forum, Mark Antony showed the crowd his bloodstained robe and read out his will. The will left money to every Roman, and the people became so angry that the killers had to flee from Rome.

Before crossing to Greece, Brutus saw a huge ghost in his tent, which said, “I am your evil spirit; you will see me at Philippi.” In 42 BC he and Cassius were defeated there by Antony and Octavian, and Brutus took his own life.
Marcus Tullius Cicero was born in 106 BC in the small town of Arpinum. His family name, Cicero, meant chickpea, because one of his forefathers had a mark on his nose like a chickpea.

As a young man Cicero had a thin voice and a weak body, and he worried that speaking would harm his health. He travelled to Athens and Rhodes to study with famous teachers, and he learned to speak in a steadier and gentler way.

Cicero served as an honest official in Sicily, and the islanders came to trust him. In 70 BC they asked him to prosecute their greedy governor Verres, and his evidence was so strong that Verres ran away.

In 63 BC Cicero was elected consul, and he soon learned that a ruined nobleman named Catiline was plotting to seize power. He faced Catiline in the Senate and asked, “How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?”

Catiline left the city to join a rebel army in the north, and he left his friends in Rome to start a fire there. Cicero caught them with letters carried by Gaulish envoys, and he arrested five of the leaders.
In the Senate Caesar spoke in favour of life in prison, because he thought that death without a trial was dangerous. Cato answered with a forceful speech, and in the end the senators voted for death.

Cicero's enemy Clodius persuaded the people to condemn him for killing citizens without a trial, and in 58 BC he left Rome in sorrow. Less than a year and a half later he was called back, and crowds along the road cheered him.
In the civil war Cicero joined Pompey, but after Pompey's defeat Caesar forgave him. In 45 BC his dear daughter Tullia died, and he spent his sad days writing books about philosophy.

After Caesar's death, Cicero gave fiery speeches against Antony, which he called Philippics, after those of Demosthenes. But Antony, Octavian and Lepidus joined forces, and made a list of their enemies, and Antony insisted on Cicero's name.

Cicero tried to escape by sea, but soldiers found him on a road near his house in December 43 BC. He told them to do their work, and they killed him, and Antony ordered that his head and hands be shown in the Forum.

After Philippi, Mark Antony took charge of the eastern lands of Rome, and he wanted money for his soldiers. In 41 BC he called Cleopatra to the city of Tarsus to explain why she had helped his enemies.

Cleopatra sailed up the river Cydnus on a golden barge with purple sails and silver oars, while flutes played. She lay under a canopy of gold, dressed like the goddess of love, and the whole city ran to the river to see her.
Plutarch says that Cleopatra's beauty was not the greatest in the world, but her charm was hard to resist. She had a sweet voice, and she could speak to many different peoples without an interpreter.

Antony spent the winter in Alexandria, where he and Cleopatra held feasts and games every day. When he was fishing, her servants secretly fixed a salted fish to his hook, and she laughed when he pulled it up.

To keep peace with Octavian, Antony married his sister Octavia, a kind and respected woman. But his war in Parthia in 36 BC was a disaster that cost thousands of lives, and he afterwards returned to Cleopatra.

In Rome, Octavian read out Antony's secret will, which left money to Cleopatra's children and asked that he be buried in Egypt. The Romans were angry that Antony had put a foreign queen before his own country, and in 32 BC they declared war on Cleopatra.

In September 31 BC the two fleets fought at Actium, and the battle was still undecided when Cleopatra's ships raised their sails and fled. Antony, who could not bear to lose her, left his fleet and sailed after her.

When Octavian reached Alexandria in 30 BC, Cleopatra shut herself in her tomb and let a message go out that she was dead. Antony believed it and wounded himself with his sword, and his servants carried him to her, and he died in her arms.

Octavian captured Cleopatra and planned to take her to Rome as a prisoner. She died a few days later, probably from poison, although Plutarch says that nobody really knew how, and Egypt then became part of Rome.

Plutarch paired each Greek hero with a Roman, such as Alexander with Caesar and Demosthenes with Cicero, and weighed their virtues and faults. In 1579 his Lives were turned into English, and Shakespeare used them for Julius Caesar, Coriolanus and Antony and Cleopatra.
C1C2: Plutarch, a Greek priest of Apollo at Delphi, begins by warning his readers that he is writing lives rather than histories. A trivial act, a casual remark or a joke, he explains, will often reveal a man's character more clearly than the greatest battle or the siege of a city. For that reason he sets his heroes side by side in pairs, one Greek and one Roman, so that readers may measure them against each other.

Plutarch was born about AD 46 in Chaeronea, a modest town in the hill country of Greece, where his family was well known. Although he travelled to Athens, to Rome and to many other places, he always came back to Chaeronea, saying that he stayed so that the little town should not grow smaller still. There, among neighbours who had known him since boyhood, he wrote most of the books that have survived.

In Athens, the old centre of Greek learning, the young Plutarch sat at the feet of the philosopher Ammonius and learned to question every claim before he accepted it. He read the poets, the historians and the thinkers of the city's golden age until their lives seemed almost as familiar to him as those of his neighbours. Years later, the heroes of that age would fill the pages that he wrote, and he would write of them as if he had known them.

By Plutarch's day, Greece had been part of the Roman world for more than two centuries, and the freedom of its cities was only a memory. He travelled to Rome, where he lectured on philosophy and made friends among senators and officials, and he confessed that he learned Latin only late in life. Living between two cultures, he came to feel that the Greeks and the Romans had more to teach each other than either admitted.

Delphi, perched on the slopes of Mount Parnassus, was the most famous shrine in the Greek world, and there Plutarch served for many years as a priest of Apollo. Pilgrims climbed its steep paths to ask the god's priestess about marriage, war and journeys, and he listened to their stories and recorded the customs of the place. The shrine taught him how deeply the ancient past still lived in the minds of the Greeks.

Plutarch's great plan was to write the lives of famous men in pairs, setting a Greek beside a Roman whose career seemed to echo his. Theseus, the legendary founder of Athens, stands beside Romulus, the founder of Rome, and Alexander, the conqueror of Asia, beside Caesar, the conqueror of Gaul. About fifty of his lives survive, and he hoped that each comparison would show readers what lay beneath the glory of the men.

Plutarch likened himself to a portrait painter, who takes the most trouble over the face and the eyes, where character shows most clearly, and gives the rest of the body a lighter touch. In the same way, he said, he would pass quickly over sieges and marches and give his best attention to the signs of the soul. The result is a set of portraits that feel less like history than like conversation with the dead.

A short saying, a jest or a passing gesture, Plutarch writes, will often reveal a man's nature more clearly than battles in which thousands fall or cities are besieged. That is why his pages are full of small stories, of what a general said to a servant or how a statesman treated his dog. Through such details a distant figure suddenly steps forward as a person we could recognise.

Plutarch explains that mapmakers, when they reach the limits of what they know, fill the margins with deserts, wild beasts and frozen seas. In the same way, he says, the earliest ages belong to poets and storytellers, and he asks the reader to forgive him for telling tales that may not be true. Wherever he can, he will say plainly which stories are history and which are only legend.

Plutarch confesses that he began to write these lives for the benefit of others, yet he soon found that he was gaining as much himself. Each hero, he says, was like a mirror in which he could arrange and improve his own life by copying the good and avoiding the bad. He invites the reader to look into the same mirror, and the first of the stories begins.

Theseus was born in Troezen, a quiet city by the sea, and there his mother Aethra and his grandfather Pittheus brought him up. His father, Aegeus, was king of distant Athens, and the boy knew him only as a name that his mother spoke with care. Pittheus, a man respected for his wisdom, took pains to teach the young prince how a ruler ought to think.

Once, when the great Hercules dined at the house of Pittheus, he laid aside his lion's skin, and the children who saw it fled in terror, thinking that a living beast lay in the room. Only the boy Theseus, who was about seven, snatched up an axe from a servant and ran at it without a sign of fear. The story shows, says Plutarch, the courage that was later to make him famous.

When Theseus reached the age of sixteen, Aethra led him to a huge rock and at last revealed his father's secret. Before leaving Troezen, Aegeus had hidden a sword and a pair of sandals beneath it, and he had ordered that the boy should come to him only when he was strong enough to lift the stone. Theseus put his shoulder to it, moved it with ease and took up the tokens that would prove who he was.

The sea route to Athens was safe, and his mother and grandfather begged him to take it, since the land road was infested with robbers and savage monsters. But Theseus had long brooded on the deeds of Hercules, whom he admired above all men, and he longed to equal them. To go by ship would have looked to him like running away, and so he took the hard road on foot.

At Epidaurus the first of the robbers stepped out to bar his path, a giant named Periphetes, who killed travellers with an iron club. Theseus met the blows with courage and skill, overcame him and took the club for his own weapon. Thereafter he carried it everywhere, just as Hercules carried the lion's skin, as the proof of what he had done.

On the narrow Isthmus lived Sinis, called the Pine-bender, who forced two pine trees to the ground and fastened his victims to them. Theseus overpowered him and punished him in exactly the same way, in keeping with his habit of paying each robber back in his own coin. It was a rough kind of justice, but the people of Greece welcomed it.

Next he killed the savage sow of Crommyon, a beast that had long terrorised the farmers of the district, though some said she was no animal but a female robber. On the cliffs above the sea he then met Sciron, who forced travellers to wash his feet and kicked them over the edge. Theseus gave him a taste of his own medicine, and the cliff road became safe at last.

At Eleusis he overcame Cercyon, a robber who challenged strangers to wrestle and killed them, and he did it by skill rather than strength, since he is said to have shaped the art of wrestling. Later he met Procrustes, who owned an iron bed that he claimed would fit any guest and who forced his victims to match its length. Theseus made the host himself lie on the bed, and the last of the great robbers was gone.

At the river Cephisus, local men cleansed him of the blood he had shed and welcomed him to a feast, and then he entered Athens. He found the city torn by quarrels and old King Aegeus under the spell of Medea, the clever sorceress, who suspected at once who the stranger might be. Fearing that a grown son would cost her own boy the throne, she began to whisper that the visitor was a spy.

At a banquet, Medea persuaded the king to offer the stranger a cup of poison, and Theseus lifted his hand to take it. Then he drew his sword, as if to carve the meat, so that his father might know it, and Aegeus, seeing the familiar handle, dashed the cup to the ground. Overjoyed, the old king embraced his son before all his people, while Medea fled the city in disgrace.

Aegeus's nephews, the sons of Pallas, had hoped to inherit the throne, and they plotted against the newly found heir, but Theseus discovered the scheme and defeated them. To win the love of the people he then went out to Marathon, captured the wild bull that was ravaging its farms and drove it alive through the streets of Athens. The citizens, who had never seen such a sight, cheered their young hero, and the bull was sacrificed to Apollo.

Minos, the powerful king of Crete, had lost a son in Attica, and he held the Athenians responsible, so he made war on them until they agreed to his terms. Every nine years they had to send seven young men and seven young women across the sea, and the tale said that a monster in a maze devoured them. When the time came to choose again, Theseus stepped forward and offered himself as one of the victims, and the people honoured his courage.

The ship that carried the young victims sailed under a black sail, as a sign of sorrow, and the whole city came down to the harbour to watch it leave. Aegeus, who feared that he would never see his son again, handed him a white sail and begged him to raise it on the return voyage if he were alive. Theseus promised to remember, and then the wind filled the sail and carried them out toward the open sea.

When the young Athenians landed in Crete, Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, saw Theseus and fell deeply in love with him. Knowing that no one had ever found a way out of the Labyrinth, she gave him a ball of thread and told him to tie one end to the entrance and unwind it as he walked. Theseus accepted the gift and promised to take her home with him as his wife if he survived.

Holding the end of the thread, Theseus walked into the Labyrinth, where every corridor led back upon itself and the air was thick with darkness and silence. At its heart he found the Minotaur, a creature with a man's body and a bull's head, and after a fierce struggle he killed it. Then, winding the thread back into a ball, he followed it to the door and led his companions into the daylight.

Under cover of darkness Theseus and the young Athenians slipped aboard their ship, damaged the Cretan vessels so that they could not follow and put out to sea with Ariadne. Plutarch notes that the ancient writers tell the story in many different ways, some saying that Theseus himself fought the monster and others giving the credit to a general named Taurus. What became of Ariadne is equally uncertain, for the accounts disagree, and Plutarch does not claim to know the truth.

On the voyage home the ships called at Delos, the sacred island of Apollo, where Theseus made offerings to the god in thanks for his escape. There he and the young Athenians performed a dance, known as the crane dance, whose turns and windings were said to copy the twisting paths of the Labyrinth. Plutarch says that the people of Delos were still performing it in his own day, many centuries later.

As the ship approached Athens, Theseus and his crew were so full of joy that they forgot to hoist the white sail that he had promised his father. Aegeus, who had been watching from a high rock for days, saw the black sail on the horizon, concluded that his son was dead and threw himself into the waves. The sea, it is said, has borne his name ever since, and Theseus came home to find himself both a king and a mourner.

As king, Theseus did something far more lasting than any combat: he persuaded the scattered villages of Attica, each with its own council and its own rulers, to give up their separate governments and become one city. He kept for himself only the command of the army and the guardianship of the laws, and he divided the people into nobles, farmers and craftsmen. The union was celebrated with a great festival, and the Athenians afterward remembered him as the founder of their city.

In his old age the fickle Athenians turned against Theseus, and he ended his days on the island of Scyros, where the local king, afraid of his fame, caused his death. Centuries later, around 475 BC, an oracle told the Athenians to bring home his bones, and the general Cimon found a grave there containing a bronze spear and a sword. He carried the remains back to Athens with great ceremony, and the people honoured them with processions and a shrine, as befitted their first hero.

Long before Rome existed, the city of Alba Longa was ruled by Numitor until his younger brother Amulius seized the throne by force. To make sure that no heir of Numitor would ever challenge him, Amulius made the old king's daughter, Rhea Silvia, a priestess who might never marry. Yet she gave birth to twin boys, and she declared that their father was the god Mars, although Plutarch says that other stories tell it differently.

Furious and afraid, Amulius commanded a servant to put the twins into a trough and leave them to the river Tiber. The servant, pitying them, set the trough at the water's edge, and when the river rose in a flood it floated the infants gently to a spot at the foot of the Palatine Hill. There the water went down again, and the trough came to rest under a wild fig tree.

According to the tale, a she-wolf came down to drink at the river, heard the babies crying and nursed them with her own milk, while a woodpecker, a bird sacred to Mars, brought them food. Faustulus, the keeper of the king's flocks, saw these wonders from a distance and, when the wolf had gone, hurried forward and carried the boys to his hut. Plutarch adds that some writers explained the wolf as a human nurse, but he gives the old story as it was told.

Raised among shepherds, the brothers grew tall, handsome and fearless, and they hunted wolves and robbers and shared out the loot among their friends. Romulus was the quicker of mind, Remus the more quarrelsome, and it was Remus who was seized one day after a brawl with the herdsmen of the exiled king Numitor and dragged before his judge. Numitor, studying the boy's face and bearing, began to wonder who he really was.

Faustulus, who had long kept the secret, now told the brothers the whole truth about their birth, and Numitor, hearing that the twins had been saved from the river, understood that these were his own grandsons. With their friends the young men entered Alba, killed the wicked Amulius, and the old king was restored to his throne amid the cheers of the citizens. But the twins preferred to be rulers rather than subjects, and they decided to found a city of their own near the place where they were raised.

Each brother preferred a different hill, Romulus the Palatine and Remus the Aventine, and neither would give way. They agreed to let the gods decide by watching the sky for birds of good omen, and Remus saw six vultures, but Romulus, a little later, saw twelve. Each insisted that the sign was in his favour, one because he had seen the birds first and the other because he had seen more, and the quarrel hardened.

Romulus marked out the boundary of his city with a bronze plough, driving a furrow around the hill, and he began to raise a wall along it. Remus mocked the low barrier and leaped across it to show how little it would protect anyone, and in the quarrel that followed he was killed. Plutarch says that some name Romulus as the killer and others a man called Celer, but all agree that Romulus mourned his brother and buried him with honour, and the city began under a shadow.

To fill his new city, Romulus opened a refuge between two sacred groves and welcomed runaways, outcasts and the homeless, until Rome swarmed with men but lacked women to marry them. When neighbouring peoples refused to give their daughters, he invited the Sabines to a festival and, at a signal, his men seized the young women who had come to watch the games. Plutarch describes it as a deed done from necessity, not from lust, and says that Romulus afterwards offered the women marriage and a share in all the rights of the city.

Titus Tatius, king of the Sabines, took up arms to win his daughters back, and after one surprise capture of Rome's citadel the armies met in a bitter battle in the valley below. Just as the slaughter reached its height, the women, now wives and mothers, ran between the lines with their hair loose and their babies in their arms, begging their fathers and their husbands to stop. Moved by this sight, the two armies made peace, and Romans and Sabines agreed to rule together under Romulus and Tatius.

After Tatius died, Romulus ruled alone for years, growing prouder and harsher with the passing of time. One day, as he reviewed his army beside a marsh, a sudden storm darkened the sky, and when the light returned the king had vanished, leaving his people to wonder whether the senators had killed him. A respected citizen named Proculus swore that Romulus had appeared to him in shining armour and told him that he had become a god, and Plutarch, doubtful of the miracle, reports it as one of the oldest legends of Rome.

Lycurgus was the younger brother of a king of Sparta, and when the king died the crown might have passed to him. But the widowed queen was expecting a child, and Lycurgus, refusing to take what belonged to his unborn nephew, lifted the baby high at a public dinner and announced that Sparta had a king. His honesty won him the respect of the citizens, though it also earned him the hatred of the queen's family, who spread rumours that he meant to seize the throne after all.

Weary of the intrigues that swirled around him, Lycurgus left Sparta and travelled widely, visiting Crete, whose laws were famous for their severity, and then Ionia, where life was soft and luxurious. He compared the two ways of life with care, and he is said to have collected the poems of Homer in Ionia and brought them to the Greeks of the mainland, who had known them only in fragments. Later writers add that he visited Egypt as well, but Plutarch notes that not everyone believed it.

Sparta, meanwhile, had sunk into disorder, with greedy rich men on one side and the angry poor on the other, and both kings and people begged Lycurgus to come home and lead them. Before he touched a single law he travelled to Delphi, where the priestess greeted him as a friend of the gods, more like a god than a man. She promised that the laws he would make were the best in the world, and armed with such a blessing he returned to Sparta and began to win over the leading citizens.

The first and greatest of Lycurgus's changes was a council of twenty-eight elders, men over sixty who served for life and who sat with the two kings to weigh every proposal. Plutarch compares this body to the water that is added to wine, since it cooled the heat of the kings on one side and the passion of the people on the other. The whole assembly of citizens could approve or reject a law by shouting, but it was not permitted to debate.

The Sparta that Lycurgus found was a place of great estates and great poverty, in which a few families owned almost everything and the rest had barely a patch of ground. Persuading the citizens to give up their holdings, he divided the land of the country into equal lots, so that each family had enough to feed it and none could look down on another. Plutarch tells of a day, long afterwards, when Lycurgus saw a field of heaped grain, smiled and said that Laconia looked like a family of brothers who had just shared an inheritance.

Not every Spartan welcomed the reforms, and the wealthy in particular grumbled, until a hot-headed young man named Alcander struck Lycurgus with a stick and blinded one of his eyes. The shocked crowd handed the culprit over to the lawgiver, but instead of taking revenge, Lycurgus took him into his house and let him see his daily life at close quarters. Within weeks Alcander had become one of his warmest admirers, and the people, who had expected a harsh punishment, learned how a strong man may use his power.

To cure the love of money, Lycurgus forbade gold and silver coin and decreed that Sparta's money should be made of iron, which was cooled in vinegar until it was too brittle to be worked into anything useful. A sum of modest value filled a room and needed a team of oxen to move it, so that theft, bribery and display were almost impossible. Foreign merchants, who could do nothing with such money, stopped visiting Sparta, and its people were spared many of the luxuries and vices of the outside world.

To end the secret feasting of the rich, Lycurgus ordered every citizen to take his meals at a common table, in groups of about fifteen, where each man brought his share of barley, wine, cheese and figs. The most famous dish was the black broth, which a tyrant of Sicily is said to have tasted and spat out, until the cook explained that he ought first to have bathed in the river Eurotas. The meals kept the rich from showing off, taught the young to listen to their elders and bound the men together as comrades.

From the age of seven a Spartan boy was taken from his family and placed in a band under a stern trainer, learning to read and write just enough for his needs but mostly to endure hunger, cold and pain. He was given only one cloak for the year and was encouraged to steal food, though he was punished severely if he was caught, not for the theft but for the clumsiness. Plutarch tells of a boy who hid a stolen fox cub under his cloak and said nothing while it bit him, since discovery was a worse fate than pain.

When the new order was complete, Lycurgus gathered the kings, the elders and the people and made them swear to keep his laws unchanged until he returned from a journey to Delphi. The god approved his work, and the lawgiver, believing that his city would be happiest if the oath could never be broken, chose to remain abroad and, as Plutarch tells it, to starve himself to death in a foreign land. He is also said to have asked that his ashes be thrown into the sea, so that no one could carry them home and claim that the oath was over, and Sparta kept his laws for hundreds of years.

Solon belonged to an old Athenian family, but his father had spent most of the family fortune on generous gifts, and the young man took to trade to earn his living. Travelling from port to port, he saw how people in different lands lived, and he wrote poems about what he saw, some playful, some grave. In one of them he wrote that he grew old always learning, and Plutarch thought the line a fine summary of his life.

Athens had lost the island of Salamis to the neighbouring city of Megara and, tired of failure, had passed a law forbidding anyone to propose another war. Solon, who could not bear the shame, pretended to be mad, ran into the market-place in a felt cap, which only the sick wore, and climbed the heralds' stone to recite a stirring poem. His verses so moved the crowd that the law was repealed, the war began again and, under Solon's guidance, Athens won the island at last.

The troubles of Athens were rooted in debt, for the poor farmers had borrowed seed and money from the rich on terms so harsh that a bad harvest could cost a man his land. Those who could not pay were reduced to labouring for their creditors, and some were sold as slaves, even abroad, while the stones that marked mortgaged fields stood in the countryside like signs of shame. The poor muttered of revolt, the rich clung to their rights, and the city seemed ready to tear itself apart.

In about 594 BC the Athenians, desperate to avoid civil war, chose Solon to reform the state with almost unlimited authority, because the poor trusted his sympathy and the rich respected his rank. He refused to make himself tyrant, though friends urged him to, and instead he cancelled the debts that were crushing the poor and forbade anyone to lend money on the security of a man's own body. The reform was known as the shaking-off of burdens, and it satisfied neither side entirely, though it saved the city.

Solon's reform was not only a matter of papers and accounts, for he also freed the Athenians who had been enslaved for debt and brought home many who had been sold in foreign countries. In one of his poems he describes how some of these exiles had wandered so long that they no longer spoke the Attic tongue, while others had endured slavery at home and trembled before their masters. Now, he says, all of them were free, and the city could at last begin to heal.

Solon divided the citizens into four classes according to what their land produced, and he reserved the highest offices for the wealthy, who were also required to serve in the army at their own expense. The poorest class, the labourers, could not hold office, but they were given a vote in the assembly and a seat on the juries that heard appeals, a right that proved far more important than it seemed. In this way he gave every man a share in the state without handing it over entirely to the crowd.

Solon replaced the harsh laws of Draco, apart from those on murder, with a new code written on wooden tablets that turned on frames, so that every citizen could read them. One of his boldest rules stated that anyone who stood aside in a civil quarrel should lose his rights as a citizen, since he believed that decent men must not stay indifferent to the safety of the state. The council and the people swore to keep the laws for ten years, and many Athenians came to Solon with suggestions and complaints.

Citizens crowded around Solon with questions, complaints and requests for changes, and he understood that he could neither please everyone nor remain to defend every clause. Using the excuse of a trading voyage, he left Athens for ten years, having made the Athenians swear that nothing would be altered until he returned. He travelled to Egypt, where he talked with learned priests, and then to Cyprus, still gathering ideas for the day when he would come home.

In Sardis, the capital of Lydia, Solon was received by Croesus, a king so wealthy that his name became a byword for riches, who showed him his treasures and asked whether he had ever met a happier man. Solon, who was too honest to flatter, replied that no one could be called happy until his life was over, for fortune turns, and no man can see what the years will bring. Croesus, who was displeased, dismissed him, but years later, when the Persian king Cyrus defeated him, he remembered the warning and called out Solon's name, and the story saved his life.

When Solon returned to Athens he found the old quarrels rising again, and the clever Peisistratus, his own relative, wounded himself and his mules and drove into the market-place, claiming that enemies had attacked him. Solon, who saw through the trick, told him he was playing Odysseus badly, but the crowd voted him a bodyguard, and with those armed men Peisistratus seized the citadel and made himself ruler of Athens. Solon, grieving but unafraid, died not long afterwards, about 560 BC, and the tyrant, to his credit, kept most of his laws.

Aristides of Athens earned the name of the Just by refusing, in public and in private, to favour a friend or take a bribe, and he lived in modest circumstances to which he seems to have been entirely indifferent. When a great Persian army landed at Marathon in 490 BC, he was one of the ten generals, and he gave up his own turn at the supreme command so that the bold Miltiades could lead the whole army. The Athenians won a famous victory, and Plutarch notes that the generosity of Aristides had helped to keep the generals united.

The Athenians had a custom called ostracism, by which they could send a man into exile for ten years if enough votes were cast against him on pieces of broken pottery. When the vote was taken against Aristides, about 482 BC, an illiterate farmer who did not know him asked him to write the name Aristides on his piece, and Aristides, without a word of protest, did so. Asked what harm the man had done to him, the farmer said none, but he was weary of hearing him called the Just, and Aristides left Athens with his dignity quite undisturbed.

Themistocles, an ambitious and brilliant man, was unable to sleep after the victory of Miltiades at Marathon, saying that the trophy would not let him rest. He saw that the Persians would return in greater force and that Athens could survive only on the sea. So he persuaded the citizens to spend the silver of their mines at Laurium, which they had meant to share out among themselves, on a great fleet of warships, and within ten years they had reason to thank him.

In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes led an enormous army against Greece, and the Athenians sent to Delphi for advice. The priestess answered that a wooden wall would not fall, and while the old men argued that she meant the fence round the Acropolis, Themistocles insisted that she meant the ships. He carried the day, and the citizens loaded their families onto boats, leaving to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis the city that they were not strong enough to defend.

As the Persian fleet approached, the Greek commanders gathered at Salamis, and most of them wanted to retreat to the Peloponnese and abandon the ships and the families of Athens. Eurybiades, the Spartan in supreme command, was so provoked by the persistence of Themistocles that he raised his stick to silence him. Themistocles, calm in the face of the insult, answered, “Strike me, but listen to me,” and the commander, impressed, heard him out and agreed to stay.

Themistocles, who wished to force the battle before the quarrelling Greeks could scatter, sent a trusted servant named Sicinnus to Xerxes with a false message that the Greeks were about to flee. The Persians moved their ships to close every escape, and that night Aristides, whom Athens had exiled, crossed from Aegina through the enemy lines to tell Themistocles that the Greeks were surrounded. The two rivals, so long at odds, forgot their quarrel on the spot, and Themistocles was able to tell the doubting commanders that there was now no choice but to fight.

At dawn the great Persian fleet rowed into the narrow strait of Salamis, where its numbers became a burden, since the ships crowded together and collided as they tried to turn. The Greek triremes, handled by sailors who knew every current and shoal, struck them from the sides and drove them in confusion across the water. Xerxes watched the destruction from a high throne on the shore, and soon afterwards he began the long journey home.

Aristides commanded the Athenians at Plataea in 479 BC, where the Greeks destroyed the Persian army that Xerxes had left behind, and afterwards he was trusted to decide what each ally should pay for the common defence. He assessed the sums so fairly that the Greeks remembered the time as a happy one, though he himself grew no richer. When he died he was so poor that the city paid for his funeral and gave his daughters dowries, and Plutarch holds up this honest poverty as his finest monument.

After Salamis the Greeks honoured Themistocles above all men, and at the Olympic Games the crowd turned from the athletes to stare at him, which led him to say that this was the harvest of all his labours. Yet his boasting made him unpopular, and the Athenians, jealous of his fame, voted to ostracise him and later accused him of treason. Hunted across Greece, he fled to King Admetus, whose wife told him to sit at the hearth with the royal child in his arms, and the king, moved by the ancient custom, refused to give him up.

Fleeing across the sea in disguise, Themistocles reached the Persian court, where he asked for a year to learn the language. Then he pleaded his case so eloquently that King Artaxerxes welcomed him as a friend and gave him three cities to support him. He lived in comfort, joking to his children that they would have been ruined had they not been ruined, and he died at Magnesia around 460 BC, though Plutarch admits that some said he took poison, and the story is uncertain.

Pericles came from one of the noblest families in Athens, and he had a long, oddly shaped head which the comic poets loved to mock, so that his statues show him wearing a helmet. His voice was gentle, his manner grave and his temper unshakable, and Plutarch tells how a rude fellow once abused him all day in the market-place and followed him to his own door, still shouting. Pericles, without turning, told a servant to take a torch and light the man safely home.

Pericles owed much of his calm to the philosopher Anaxagoras, who taught him to look for natural causes rather than to tremble at omens and eclipses. Once a ram with a single horn was brought from his farm, and the seer Lampon declared that it meant that power in Athens would be united in one man. Anaxagoras, however, examined the animal's skull and showed that its brain had grown in an unusual shape, and Plutarch says with characteristic fairness that both men were right, one explaining the cause and the other the meaning.

To keep the respect of the people, Pericles all but gave up the pleasures of a rich man's social life, declining invitations to dinner and appearing in public only on the road to the market-place and the council house. When he did go to a kinsman's wedding feast, he left as soon as the wine was poured, since he believed that familiarity breeds contempt. In this manner he made himself rare and admired, and he gradually became the leading man of Athens.

To give the poor a real share in public life, Pericles introduced pay for jurors, so that a craftsman or a farmer could spend a day in the courts without ruining his family. His rivals complained that he was buying the favour of the crowd with the city's money, and some said he was spoiling the character of the people. Yet Athens flourished under his guidance, and the humblest citizen came to feel that the state was truly his own.

Pericles persuaded the Athenians to use the wealth of their empire to raise the Parthenon and other glorious buildings on the Acropolis, under the direction of the architects Ictinus and Callicrates. Thousands of stonecutters, carpenters, bronze-workers and carvers found employment, and the works rose with astonishing speed. Plutarch marvels that they seemed at once both fresh and ancient, for they had the beauty of age on the day they were finished.

The sculptor Pheidias, a close friend of Pericles, directed the works on the Acropolis and made a towering statue of Athena covered with gold and ivory. Pericles's enemies, unable to attack the great man directly, accused his friend of stealing some of the gold, but the gold had been fitted so that it could be removed and weighed, and the whole amount was found. Pheidias was then charged with impiety, because he had carved his own portrait and that of Pericles on the goddess's shield, and he died in prison.

In his private life Pericles loved Aspasia, a woman of Miletus who was famous for her intelligence and wit, and he lived with her after parting from his first wife. Plutarch says that he kissed her every morning when he left for the market and again when he returned, and that even Socrates visited her with his friends to hear her talk. His enemies, who could not touch him directly, prosecuted her on a charge of impiety, and Pericles himself pleaded for her in court, weeping, and secured her acquittal.

When war with Sparta broke out in 431 BC, Pericles urged the Athenians not to fight on land against the finest infantry in Greece, but to bring the country people inside the long walls and to rely on their fleet. The strategy was sound, yet the crowding of so many people into the city in the heat of summer made it a breeding-ground for disease, and a dreadful plague broke out. Thousands died, the survivors lost heart, and the citizens, forgetting their trust in him, turned their anger on Pericles.

The plague took many of Pericles's friends and relatives, and finally both of his legitimate sons, one after the other, so that his own house was left almost empty. He bore the first losses with the calm that he had shown all his life, but at the funeral of Paralus, as he placed the wreath on the body, he broke down and wept aloud. The Athenians had never seen him do this, and the citizens, who had fined him and removed him from command, soon recalled him and elected him general once again.

In 429 BC Pericles himself fell ill, and as he lay dying his friends gathered around the bed, listing his victories and the trophies he had set up for Athens. The sick man, whom they supposed to be unconscious, interrupted them to say that these were shared with luck and common to many generals. His truest claim to honour, he said, was that no living Athenian had put on mourning because of him, and the citizens, who had so often turned against him, soon felt his loss.

Alcibiades was exceptionally handsome, clever and rich, and after his father was killed in battle he was brought up in the house of his guardian Pericles. Even as a boy he was used to getting his own way, and when a heavy cart interrupted his game of dice in the street, he lay down in front of the horses. He told the driver to go on if he dared, and the driver, appalled, drew back, while the other children, who had scattered at once, came running back to admire him.

As a boy, Alcibiades was never content to lose, and when a stronger opponent had him pinned in a wrestling match, he bit the other's arm so hard that the boy cried out that he bit like a woman. Alcibiades replied, quite unabashed, that he bit like a lion, and the story went round Athens as a sign of his fierce pride. He also refused to learn the flute, saying that it distorted the face and that a gentleman should speak rather than blow, and his example was so influential that the flute went out of fashion among the young.

Alcibiades was surrounded by admirers who flattered his beauty and his ambition, but the philosopher Socrates was the only man who could shame him. When Socrates spoke of how little he really knew and how much he lacked in virtue, the young man was moved to tears, and he declared that his heart leapt at those words. Yet the lure of power and applause was strong, and again and again he escaped from his teacher, like a runaway slave, back into the arms of his flatterers.

Alcibiades once bought a magnificent dog for an enormous sum, and to everyone's astonishment he cut off its tail, the finest part of the animal. When his friends protested, he said that this was exactly what he had wanted, since it meant that Athens would gossip about the dog instead of saying worse things about him. The story shows both his reckless charm and his habit of managing public opinion, and Plutarch cannot help smiling at it.

When Athens fought at Potidaea, Alcibiades and Socrates shared a tent and served in the same ranks, and when the young man was wounded, Socrates stood over him and saved both his life and his armour. The generals wanted to give the prize for valour to Alcibiades, but Socrates urged them to honour his friend instead, in the hope of encouraging him in the path of virtue. Some years afterward, at the rout of Delium, Alcibiades, who was on horseback, returned the favour by riding alongside Socrates and guarding him as he retreated on foot.

In 415 BC the Athenians were seized with a longing to conquer Sicily, and Alcibiades fed their ambition with talk of gaining first Sicily, then Carthage and perhaps all Italy. The cautious Nicias, who foresaw the dangers of a war so far from home, argued in vain against him, and the vote was carried by popular enthusiasm. A magnificent fleet sailed from the harbour, its ships crowded with the best of the Athenian young men, and the whole city came to the shore to wish it well.

Shortly before the fleet sailed, the stone statues of Hermes that stood at street corners all over Athens were mutilated in a single night. Enemies of Alcibiades, who was also accused of mocking the sacred mysteries, laid the blame on him, and once he had reached Sicily he was summoned home for trial. Realising that his enemies were waiting for him, he slipped away from his escort at Thurii, and the Athenians condemned him to death in his absence, whereupon he vowed to show them that he was still alive.

In Sparta, Alcibiades became a chameleon, for he wore his hair cropped, bathed in cold water and ate coarse bread and black broth, and so charmed the Spartans that they could hardly believe he had ever known luxury. He advised them to send a commander to help the besieged city of Syracuse and to fortify Decelea, a base from which they could harass Athens all year round. Both pieces of advice proved ruinous to his native city, but his success made him enemies, and he soon left Sparta for the court of a Persian governor.

After helping the Athenian fleet win a string of victories, Alcibiades sailed home in 407 BC, still half afraid of his old enemies, until he saw his friends and relatives crowding the harbour with garlands and shouts of welcome. The assembly cancelled the sentence against him, made him supreme commander by land and sea, and he marked his return by leading the sacred procession to Eleusis under the protection of his soldiers. For a short time it seemed that the hero of Athens had at last come home for good.

Alcibiades left his helmsman Antiochus in command during a short absence, and when Antiochus rashly gave battle at Notium and lost, the Athenians, always quick to blame their favourite, took away his command and sent him into exile once more. He retired to a fortified village in Phrygia, where in 404 BC a band of assassins, too fearful to attack him openly, surrounded his house at night and set it on fire. Alcibiades burst out with a dagger in his hand and, driven back by showers of arrows, fell and died, one of the most brilliant and the most wasted lives in Plutarch's gallery.

Demosthenes was only seven years old when his father, a wealthy maker of swords, died, and the guardians who managed the estate wasted most of it. As a young man he studied the art of speaking with the orator Isaeus and then took his guardians to court, where he pleaded his own case and won, although he recovered only a small part of his fortune. The experience, however, had given him a taste for the platform, and he resolved to become a public speaker.

When Demosthenes first spoke to the Athenian assembly, his weak voice, his awkward sentences and his habit of running out of breath made the audience jeer, and he went home in despair. A friendly old man told him that his speeches were as fine as those of Pericles, and then the actor Satyrus recited the same lines first plainly and then with feeling. Demosthenes saw at once how much of an orator's power lies in his voice and his gestures, and from that day he resolved to train himself with relentless discipline.

Determined to conquer his stammer and his shortness of breath, Demosthenes practised speaking with pebbles in his mouth and recited long passages of verse as he ran uphill. On the shore he declaimed against the roar of the waves, so that no uproar in the assembly would ever put him off, and at home he rehearsed his gestures in front of a large mirror. Plutarch cites many witnesses to these habits, and says that Demosthenes laboured harder than anyone to turn himself into an orator.

He built himself a small study underground, where he rehearsed his speeches and practised his delivery for weeks and even months at a time. To make sure that nothing tempted him out of doors, he shaved one half of his head, so that shame would keep him at his books. His rival Pytheas sneered that his arguments smelled of lamp oil, and Demosthenes answered that his lamp and Pytheas's lamp saw very different things.

King Philip of Macedon was growing stronger by the year, seizing city after city in the north of Greece and extending his influence into the south. Demosthenes, convinced that Philip would never rest until the Greeks had lost their freedom, delivered speeches that urged the Athenians to arm themselves and resist, and these fiery speeches became known as the Philippics. Many of his listeners preferred comfort to danger, and they accused him of seeing enemies everywhere.

When Philip marched south and threatened Athens itself, Demosthenes rushed to Thebes, an old rival of Athens, where Philip's envoys were already pleading for the Thebans' neutrality. His speech, which Plutarch compares to a flame that consumed every other argument, persuaded the Thebans to ally themselves with Athens, and the proud people of both cities joined to resist the king. It was perhaps the greatest triumph of Demosthenes's career, and it led directly to the fatal battle.

In 338 BC the armies of Philip and the Greeks met at Chaeronea, the small town where Plutarch himself was born, and the Macedonians won a decisive victory in which the young Alexander commanded the cavalry. Philip, drunk with success, danced over the field and mocked the speeches of Demosthenes until the orator Demades reproached him, saying that fortune had cast him as Agamemnon but he was acting like Thersites. The king, sobered, treated the defeated Athenians with moderation, and the ancient freedom of the Greek cities was gone.

After the destruction of Thebes in 335 BC, Alexander demanded that the Athenians hand over ten of their leading orators, among them Demosthenes, whom he blamed for stirring up resistance. Demosthenes rose and told the assembly the fable of the sheep who were asked by the wolves to give up the sheepdogs that guarded them, and he warned that the orators were the watchdogs of the city. The Athenians hesitated, and in the end Demades and other friends of Alexander begged the king for mercy and secured the safety of the speakers.

When Alexander died in 323 BC, Demosthenes was recalled from exile and led the call for a new revolt against Macedon, but the general Antipater defeated the Greeks and demanded that the leading orators be given up. The Athenians, under pressure, condemned their old champion to death in his absence, and Demosthenes, who had gone into hiding, slipped away by sea toward a small island. Wherever he went, he was followed by an agent named Archias, who had been hired to bring him back.

On the island of Calauria, Demosthenes took refuge in the temple of Poseidon, but Archias, the agent of Antipater, followed him and tried to coax him out with kind words. Pretending that he wanted to write a last letter, the old orator put the pen to his lips and bit it, swallowing the poison that he had hidden in it. Then he stepped from the sanctuary, so that its holy ground would not be stained, and fell dead, and his death in 322 BC ended the line of free Athenian speakers.

Alexander was born in 356 BC, the son of Philip, king of Macedon, and his wife Olympias, a fiery woman from Epirus. His father's family claimed descent from Hercules, and his mother's from Achilles, and so the child grew up believing that he belonged among heroes. Plutarch adds a story that on the night of his birth the great temple of Artemis at Ephesus burned down, and that a witty writer said the goddess had been too busy attending the birth to save her own house.

As a boy Alexander was brave, ambitious and a swift runner, and when friends urged him to enter the footrace at the Olympic Games, he replied that he would run only if his rivals were kings. Whenever news came that his father had taken a city or won a great battle, he would sigh to his playmates that Philip would use up all the glory and leave nothing great for him to do. His companions, who thought only of power and riches, did not understand that he longed for deeds, not possessions.

A horse dealer once brought the magnificent black horse Bucephalus to Philip, but the animal reared at every rider, and the king ordered it taken away as hopelessly wild. Alexander, still a boy, noticed that the horse was afraid of its own shadow, and he turned it gently toward the sun, stroked it and leaped onto its back. Philip, who had watched in silence, wept with joy and told his son to find a kingdom large enough for himself, because Macedon was too small for him.

Philip invited the philosopher Aristotle, the most famous scholar in Greece, to teach his son in a quiet grove at Mieza, where the young prince and his friends studied ethics, politics, medicine and poetry. Alexander learned to love books, and above all Homer's Iliad, a copy of which he later kept under his pillow beside his dagger. He used to say that he owed his life to his father but a good life to his teacher.

Once, while Philip was away, ambassadors from the Persian king arrived at the Macedonian court, and the boy Alexander entertained them with such charm that they were delighted. He did not ask childish questions about gold or palaces but wanted to know the length of the roads into Asia, what sort of man their king was and how he treated his enemies. The envoys marvelled that the great reputation of Philip seemed small beside the ambition of his son.

Although he was only eighteen, Alexander commanded one wing of the army at Chaeronea, and Plutarch reports that he was the first to break the Sacred Band of Thebes, an elite corps of three hundred men famous for its courage. The Thebans fought to the end where they stood, and when the king saw them lying in their ranks, he wept and praised their bravery. Plutarch, who lived near the field, writes that in his own day people still pointed out an oak tree beside the river where Alexander's tent had stood.

When Philip married a young Macedonian woman, her uncle Attalus, in his cups, urged the guests to pray for a legitimate heir to the throne. Alexander, stung by the insult to his mother, flung his cup at Attalus, and Philip, in a rage, drew his sword and rushed at his son, only to stumble and fall to the floor. Alexander looked down at his father with scorn and said that here was the man who meant to cross from Europe to Asia and could not even cross from one couch to another.

In 336 BC, while Philip was entering a theatre during the wedding celebrations of his daughter, a young bodyguard named Pausanias, who nursed a bitter grievance, struck him down. Alexander, just twenty years old, was proclaimed king by the army, and he soon found himself surrounded by dangers, for the Greek cities and the northern tribes saw a chance to rebel. He faced these enemies with such energy and skill that within a short time every threat had been brought under control.

When Thebes rebelled in 335 BC, Alexander stormed the city and razed it to the ground, intending that its fate should teach the Greeks never to defy him again. The decision was harsh, and Plutarch admits that the king later regretted the cruelty, but he gave orders that the temples, the priests and the house of the poet Pindar should be spared. The Greeks, who loved the verse of Pindar, noticed that even in his anger the young conqueror had shown respect for a poet.

At Corinth the Greek cities, whether willingly or not, elected Alexander their commander against Persia, and crowds of statesmen and philosophers came to congratulate him. Only Diogenes, who lived like a beggar in a large jar by the city wall, took no notice, so Alexander went to find him and asked whether he could help. Diogenes replied, “Only stand out of my sun,” and Alexander, struck by his freedom, told his friends that he would choose to be Diogenes if he were not Alexander.

In the spring of 334 BC Alexander led his army across the Hellespont into Asia, with, according to Plutarch's sources, very few supplies and only a small sum of money in the treasury. Before leaving Macedon he had given away most of the royal estates to his friends, and when Perdiccas asked what he had kept for himself, the young king replied simply that he had kept hope. Perdiccas, understanding the answer, refused his own share, saying that those who shared the king's hope should share his labour as well.

On the way south, Alexander went out of his way to visit the plain of Troy, where he poured offerings at the tombs of the heroes and placed a wreath on the grave of Achilles. He called Achilles a lucky man, because he had found a faithful friend in life and a great poet to proclaim his glory after death. It was the kind of fame that Alexander himself desired, and a reader may well guess that he already imagined a poet singing of his own deeds.

At the river Granicus, in 334 BC, the Persian governors waited on the steep far bank, and Alexander, ignoring the cautious advice of his older generals, plunged into the current. His white-plumed helmet made him an easy mark, and a Persian noble had already raised his axe to cut him down when his friend Cleitus rode in and struck the man first. The Persians broke and fled, and Alexander sent three hundred captured suits of armour to Athens as an offering to the goddess.

In the city of Gordium stood an ancient cart whose yoke was bound with a knot so cunningly tied that no one could find its ends, and a legend promised that whoever untied it would rule all Asia. Alexander, after studying it for a time, drew his sword and cut through the knot, and the local people said that the prophecy had been fulfilled. Some writers say that he simply drew out the pin that held it, but the tale of the sword has been told of Alexander ever since.

At Issus in 333 BC, Alexander routed the great army of King Darius, who fled in such haste that he left behind his mother, his wife and his daughters. When Alexander entered the royal tent, he found baths, golden vessels and sweet perfumes, and he remarked drily that this was apparently what it meant to be a king. Plutarch says that he treated the captive women with a delicacy that surprised everyone, giving them the honours of queens and assuring them that Darius was alive and that none of them had cause for fear.

In 332 BC the island city of Tyre, proud of its sea walls and its fleet, refused to open its gates to Alexander. He ordered his army to build a great causeway of earth and stone across the water, and the siege dragged on for months until, as Plutarch reports, Alexander dreamed of a dancing satyr, a half-goat spirit of the woods. The seers pointed out that the Greek word for satyr could be split into the words for Tyre is yours, and the encouraged army broke into the city.

In 331 BC, in Egypt, Alexander decided to found a great Greek city beside the sea, and the architect Dinocrates marked out its walls on the ground. When the supplies of chalk ran out, the workmen used barley meal from the soldiers' rations, and flocks of birds swooped down and ate it all. Alexander was uneasy until his seers explained that the city would one day be rich and would feed many peoples, and so it proved, for Alexandria became one of the wonders of the ancient world.

Not satisfied with his conquests, Alexander made a long journey across the desert to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa, guided, the stories said, by two ravens that showed him the way when a sandstorm had hidden the road. The priest greeted him as the son of the god, which suited the king's imagination, though Plutarch is careful to say that Alexander did not take it too seriously. In a letter he wrote that Zeus is the father of all men, but he makes the best of them especially his own.

On the morning of the great battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC, the Macedonian officers found their commander so deeply asleep that old Parmenio had to wake him. When they expressed astonishment, Alexander replied that there was nothing strange in it, for Darius had at last gathered all his forces in one place, and the long chase was nearly over. By evening the Persian king had fled once more, and the empire of Persia lay open to the conqueror.

After Babylon and Susa, Alexander reached Persepolis, where he found such treasures that thousands of mules and camels were needed to carry them away. During a drunken banquet, the Athenian woman Thais urged the king to set fire to the palace of Xerxes, who had once burned Athens, and the guests ran out with torches. Plutarch says that Alexander quickly repented and ordered the flames put out, though by then much of the palace was lost.

In the pursuit of Darius, the Macedonians marched through a burning land, and Alexander himself was tormented by thirst. Some soldiers who had found water in skins carried by mules brought him a helmetful, but he saw the faces of his thirsty cavalry turn toward him, and he handed it back untouched. If he drank alone, he said, the others would lose heart, and the men, moved by his self-control, shouted to him to lead them on, for they felt neither hunger nor thirst while they had such a king.

Darius's own officers, led by the satrap Bessus, seized the unlucky king and then, as Alexander's cavalry closed in, wounded him and left him dying in a cart on the road. When Alexander arrived, the Persian king was already dead, and the young conqueror, moved to tears by his fate, took off his own cloak and laid it over the body. He sent the body to be buried among the Persian kings, and he swore to punish the men who had murdered their master.

At a drunken banquet in 328 BC, the old officer Cleitus began to praise Philip at the expense of Alexander and, holding out his right hand, reminded the king that it was this hand that had saved him at the Granicus. Blind with rage and wine, Alexander snatched a spear from a guard and killed him on the spot, and then, as soon as he understood what he had done, he fell into a passion of remorse. For three days he lay in his room, refusing food and drink, until his friends persuaded him that the deed had been destined by fate.

In 326 BC Alexander reached the Hydaspes river in India, where King Porus waited with an army of war elephants on the farther bank, and he crossed by night in a thunderstorm to take the enemy by surprise. Porus, a man of great height who fought on bravely until he was wounded, was brought before the victor, who asked him how he wished to be treated. Porus answered, “Like a king,” and when Alexander pressed him for more, he said that everything was contained in that one phrase, and the delighted conqueror let him keep his kingdom.

Bucephalus, the horse that Alexander had tamed as a boy, had carried him through every campaign, and it would let no other rider mount, though it would kneel for its master. After the battle with Porus the great horse died, whether of its wounds or of old age, for it was about thirty years old, and Alexander mourned him as he would have mourned a friend. He founded a city on the river bank and named it Bucephala, so that the horse's name should live.

After so many years of fighting, the Macedonians were exhausted and homesick, and when they heard that mighty kings with elephants ruled beyond the next river, they refused to go on. Alexander shut himself in his tent for days, hoping that they would change their minds, but when he saw that they would not, he gave way. At last, with great reluctance, he ordered the whole army to turn around and march back toward the sea.

Alexander built a fleet and sailed down the rivers of India toward the ocean, fighting the tribes along the banks. At a town of the Malli he leaped alone over the wall in his eagerness, and an arrow pierced his armour and lodged in his chest, so that his friends feared that he was dying. He was carried out on a shield, and when he recovered and showed himself to his soldiers, the army greeted him with such joy that many men wept.

On the return journey to Persia, Alexander led a large part of his army through the Gedrosian desert, a barren coast of burning sand where there was little food and almost no water. The march lasted for about two months, and many soldiers and camp followers died of thirst, heat and exhaustion before the survivors reached cultivated land. Plutarch, who generally admires Alexander, counts it among the heaviest losses of his career.

At Susa in 324 BC Alexander held a splendid mass wedding, taking a daughter of Darius as his own wife and giving Persian brides to many of his officers, in the hope of joining the two peoples in one. Soon afterwards, at Ecbatana, his closest friend Hephaestion fell ill and died, and the king was so crushed that he refused food for days and ordered a funeral of astonishing splendour. From that time, Plutarch says, he grew restless and fearful and looked for omens in everything.

In June 323 BC, after a banquet and a long fever, Alexander lay dying at Babylon, and the soldiers who demanded to see him were allowed to file past his bed in silence. He could no longer speak, but he greeted each man with a movement of his head or eyes, and he died at the age of thirty-two. Asked to whom he left his kingdom, he is said to have answered that it should go to the strongest, and the empire he had won in a decade soon broke apart among his generals.

Gaius Marcius, a young Roman of noble family, lost his father in childhood and was brought up by his widowed mother Volumnia, who taught him to value honour above everything. He grew into a soldier of great courage who feared no danger and who won prizes for bravery almost before he had a beard.
