Plutarch says that this very strength of spirit, untamed by teaching, made him stubborn and a poor friend to ordinary people.

In those years the poor of Rome, weighed down by debts and angry at the rich, marched out of the city and settled on a hill beyond its walls. The senators sent the old and respected Menenius, who told them the fable of the body whose limbs rebelled against the belly for keeping all the food, only to find that they starved. The people understood the lesson, returned to the city, and were given their own officers, called tribunes, to protect them.

When the Romans besieged the Volscian city of Corioli, the defenders came out to fight, and Marcius drove them back so fiercely that he pushed into the gates with only a handful of followers behind him. Left almost alone among the enemy, he fought his way through the streets and held them off until the other Romans caught up and took the town. The moment was so wild that Plutarch says he seemed to be fighting more than one man's battle.

After the victory the consul Cominius praised Marcius in front of the whole army, offered him a share of the treasure, and gave him the name Coriolanus, which the Romans used from then on. The new hero refused the gold, accepted a horse, and asked only that one prisoner, a poor man who had once been his host, should be set free. The soldiers cheered him for refusing money, which Plutarch thinks was worth more than any prize.

According to Roman custom, a man who stood for the consulship went among the voters in a plain robe, showed the scars of his wounds, and asked for their support. Coriolanus did so with so little grace, and with so plain a scorn for the people he was asking, that the crowd, which had begun by honouring him, turned against him. His enemies were quick to see that his pride would serve them better than any argument.

When famine came to Rome, ships brought grain from abroad, and the senators wondered whether to give it to the hungry or to sell it at a high price. Coriolanus rose and said that the people should not be fed cheaply unless they agreed to give up their tribunes, whom he blamed for the city's weakness. The tribunes, who had been waiting for just such a remark, called him before the assembly to answer for his words.

The assembly condemned Coriolanus to permanent exile, and the poor of Rome were so delighted that they filled the streets with shouting, as they had not done even for a great victory over an enemy. He bore the sentence calmly, comforted his weeping mother and wife at the door of his house, and walked out of the city with only a few friends, saying that the world was wide. Plutarch notes that in his heart, however, anger was already working like a poison.

In his anger Coriolanus made for Antium, where he walked, wrapped in his cloak, into the house of Tullus Aufidius, the Volscian general who had often fought him, and sat in silence by the hearth. When Aufidius asked who he was, he uncovered his face and offered his sword against the Rome that had cast him out, or else his head, to be taken as a prize if his old enemy preferred. Aufidius, who admired courage even in a foe, took his hand and welcomed him as an ally.

Within a short time the Volscian army, now led by Coriolanus and Aufidius together, burned the fields of Rome's people and made camp only a few miles from the city. The terrified senate sent his oldest friends to beg him to make peace, and then the priests in their sacred robes, but he answered all of them coldly and told them to accept his terms. Panic spread among the Romans, and many of the women ran to the temples to pray.

At last the women of Rome went out to the Volscian camp, led by Volumnia, who brought his wife Virgilia and his two small sons. She asked him whether he really meant to march over the body of the woman who had borne him, and Coriolanus, who had resisted the envoys and the priests, could not resist his mother. He embraced her, said, “Mother, you have saved Rome, but you have lost your son,” and led his army away, to be killed by the Volscians, according to Plutarch, not long afterwards.

Pyrrhus, the ambitious king of Epirus, who claimed descent from Achilles, was invited by the Greek city of Tarentum to lead its war against Rome. His adviser Cineas asked him, step by step, what he would do after each conquest, and Pyrrhus named Italy, then Sicily, then Africa, until at last he said that he would rest and drink with his friends. Cineas asked why he should not do that now, but the king would not listen.

In 280 BC Pyrrhus crossed to Italy with an army of about twenty thousand foot soldiers, three thousand horsemen and twenty elephants, and he met the Romans in battle at Heraclea. The Romans fought bravely, but neither they nor their horses had ever seen such beasts, and the elephants decided the day. Pyrrhus, who walked over the field afterwards and counted his own dead, remarked that his victory had cost him many of his best friends.

When the Romans sent the poor but honest Fabricius to talk about prisoners, Pyrrhus offered him a large sum of gold, and Fabricius refused it as calmly as he would have refused a gift from a stranger. The next day the king hid an elephant behind a curtain and had it raise its trunk over the Roman's head, but Fabricius told him calmly that neither the gold nor the beast had moved him. Pyrrhus, filled with respect for this plain and honest man, said that he wished all Romans were as steady as Fabricius.

At Asculum in 279 BC Pyrrhus won a second battle against the Romans, but his army had lost its best officers and many of its soldiers, while Rome could call on new recruits whenever it wished. “One more victory like that,” he is said to have told his friends, “and we shall be ruined,” and before long he left Italy altogether. Plutarch adds that he was killed some years later at Argos, in a street fight, when an old woman threw a roof tile down on his head.

Quintus Fabius Maximus, who had been so quiet and slow as a child that his companions called him the Lamb, grew into a man of calm judgment who was never carried away by anger or fear. When Hannibal came down from the Alps and destroyed a Roman army at Lake Trasimene in 217 BC, the frightened Romans turned to him and made him dictator. Plutarch reports that he began by asking the gods to protect the city, as if the first battle must be won in the temples.

Fabius understood that Hannibal's army could not be beaten in the open field, so he followed it along the hills, cut off its supplies and refused every challenge to fight. The Romans, who wanted a quick revenge, called him Hannibal's schoolteacher and a coward, and even some of his officers urged him to be more bold. He bore the scorn without complaint, because he cared more for the safety of his country than for his own good name.

One summer Fabius closed the mountain passes around a plain where Hannibal's army was camping, and he believed that the enemy was trapped. That night Hannibal had bundles of burning twigs tied to the horns of about two thousand oxen and driven toward the hills, and the Roman guards, seeing the lights, left their posts to chase them. While the guards were distracted by the strange lights on the hills, the Carthaginians slipped quietly through the unguarded pass and escaped with their whole army.

The Romans, angry with Fabius, made his deputy Minucius equal to him in rank, and the two men divided the army between them. Minucius promptly rushed into battle, was caught in an ambush by Hannibal, and would have been destroyed if Fabius had not come to his aid with fresh troops. Humbled by the rescue, Minucius greeted the old general as a father, and put himself under his command again.

Fabius soon gave up his office, and the Romans who followed him, tired of waiting, marched out in 216 BC to meet Hannibal at Cannae in open battle. The result was the worst defeat in the history of the city, in which something like fifty thousand Romans were killed, and the survivors who staggered home were stunned. Only then did the people begin to understand that Fabius's patient method, which they had mocked, was the one that could save them.

When the senators refused to pay the ransom for some Roman prisoners held by Hannibal, Fabius sold his own estate and paid for their freedom from his own pocket. He lived on, and honoured as the shield of Rome, he died at a great age in 203 BC, a few years before Hannibal finally left Italy. Plutarch says that the people paid for his funeral by each giving the smallest coin, as children might do for a father.

Marcus Porcius Cato, born about 234 BC to a family of farmers in the Italian countryside, spent his youth working his own small field with his own hands. In the evening he sat down to the same coarse bread and cheap wine as his labourers, and he dressed as they did, because he believed that luxury was the first step toward ruin. Plutarch says that his neighbours, who respected a man with no pride, thought highly of him for it.

While Cato was still very young, Hannibal's army was ravaging Italy, and he went to war as soon as he was old enough, serving with the Roman legions in several campaigns. He carried his own equipment, drank water on the march and ate whatever the common soldiers ate, so that his officers, who were used to complaints from young nobles, were at first surprised and then full of admiration. He soon gained a reputation for courage and endurance that, in Plutarch's account, he never lost.

A nobleman named Valerius Flaccus, who owned land beside Cato's farm, noticed the young man's sharp mind and honest manner and urged him to try his fortune in Rome. Cato did so, speaking in the law courts on behalf of his neighbours and friends, and the force and bluntness of his speech made people stop to listen. He soon rose from one office to the next, and his rough country manner became his strength instead of a weakness.

In 195 BC Cato was elected consul, a very great honour for a man with no famous ancestors, and the Senate sent him to Spain, where the local tribes were in revolt. By energy and cunning, and by a good deal of hard fighting, he beat them in the field, took their towns and restored peace to the province. When he returned to Rome, he was granted a triumph, a splendid parade through the city that every Roman soldier dreamed of.

Years later, in 191 BC, Cato was sent to Greece as an officer in the war against King Antiochus, who had taken up a strong position at the narrow pass of Thermopylae. In the old way of the Persians who had once beaten Leonidas there, he led a small force at night along a steep mountain path and fell on the enemy's camp from behind. Antiochus's army broke and ran, and Cato, delighted, claimed that the victory belonged to him and not to the general.

When Cato was elected censor in 184 BC, he took the post as seriously as a doctor takes an operation, for the office gave him the power to judge the conduct of every citizen. He struck the name of a distinguished former consul from the list of senators, taxed expensive clothes, jewels and carriages heavily, and cut off the water that the rich had piped into their private gardens. The people, who admired his courage, put up a statue of him, but his many enemies never forgave him.

In 155 BC three famous philosophers came from Athens to Rome on a diplomatic mission, and the young men of the city flocked to hear them speak, delighted by arguments that could make either side of a question seem right. Cato, who believed that Rome had conquered the world by sturdy habits and not by clever talk, urged the Senate to settle their business and send them home as quickly as possible. In his old age, Plutarch says, he nonetheless began to study Greek himself, though only a little.

On a visit to Carthage to help settle a border quarrel, Cato was alarmed to see that the city, which Rome had defeated years before, had grown rich again, with a large population, plenty of weapons and a strong fleet. Back in the Senate he shook out the fold of his toga and let some ripe figs roll onto the floor, then told the senators that the country that grew such fruit lay only three days' sail from Rome. The point went home, and from that day he saw Carthage as the enemy that would one day return.

From that day Cato brought every speech he made to the same end, whether the topic was farms, taxes or foreign affairs, with the words that, in his opinion, Carthage must be destroyed. His rival Scipio Nasica used to answer, just as stubbornly, that Carthage should be spared, because the fear of an old enemy kept Rome from growing lazy. Whether the words of Cato alone brought on the third war against Carthage is uncertain, but the Romans never forgot his sentence.

Cato remained vigorous almost to the end, writing books on farming and history and speaking in the Senate, and, in Plutarch's report, he even took a young second wife and had a baby son when he was already old. He died in 149 BC, about eighty-five years old, and so he did not live to see the war that he had demanded. Three years later, in 146 BC, the Romans took Carthage and destroyed it, and its land became a Roman province.

When the young Julius Caesar sailed to Rhodes to study public speaking, pirates seized his ship near a small island off the coast of Asia, and demanded twenty talents of silver as a ransom. Caesar laughed at them for not knowing whom they had caught, and said that they should ask for fifty, which was a sum worthy of him. He then sent his friends to the cities to collect the money, and stayed behind with only a doctor and two servants.

For about forty days the young Roman lived among those rough men, and he behaved so little like a captive that he took part in their games and exercises as if he were the master of the ship. He wrote poems and speeches and read them aloud, calling the pirates ignorant barbarians when they did not admire them, and when he wished to sleep, he sent word that they must be quiet. Smiling, he often told them that when he was free he would have every one of them put to death on a cross.

As soon as the ransom had been paid and he was safe on land, Caesar fitted out a small fleet at the harbour of Miletus and sailed straight back to the island where the pirates lay at anchor. He captured most of them, recovered his money, and brought the prisoners to the governor of Asia, who hesitated, and so Caesar carried out his promise himself. Plutarch adds that, because they had been kind to him, he first had their lives ended quickly, as an act of mercy.

Some years later, while he was serving as a governor in Spain, Caesar was reading about the deeds of Alexander the Great, and he suddenly fell silent and began to weep. His friends asked him why, and he explained that at his age Alexander had already conquered so much of the world, while he himself had done nothing worth remembering. From then on, Plutarch says, he hunted for chances to make a name, and his ambition was never at rest.

Caesar understood that no single man could rule in Rome without friends, so he secretly joined Pompey, the great general, and Crassus, the richest man in the city, in an alliance that all three could use against their enemies. With their help he was elected consul in 59 BC, and when his year in office ended, he took command of the Roman provinces in Gaul, which stretched over the Alps toward the barbarian lands beyond. Many Romans saw that he was now a danger, but few dared to say so openly.

In the next eight years or so, Caesar conquered the whole of Gaul, bridged the river Rhine in a matter of days, and crossed the sea to Britain, which no Roman general had done before him. His soldiers, who followed him through snow, rivers and forests, loved him because he shared their hardships and rewarded courage wherever he found it. Plutarch says that the men seemed unbeatable, and that even an ordinary soldier, if Caesar's honour was at stake, would face any danger.

The alliance between the three men had been held together by Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's loving wife, and when she died in 54 BC, the bond between her husband and her father began to loosen. A year later Crassus, who had gone to fight the Parthians, was killed in battle, and the two remaining rivals were left face to face. Encouraged by Caesar's enemies, the Senate then ordered him to disband his army and return to Rome as a private citizen.

In January 49 BC Caesar halted at the Rubicon, the little river that marked the boundary of his province, and he stood in silence for some time, weighing what it would mean if he crossed it with his army. Then, as Plutarch tells it, he said to his companions, “Let the die be cast,” and led his soldiers over the water and on toward Rome. His surprised enemies, who had expected him to move slowly, fled the city in panic.

In the summer of 48 BC the two armies met on the plain of Pharsalus, where Pompey, with twice as many soldiers, felt so sure of victory that his friends quarrelled over who would replace Caesar as high priest. Caesar's veterans, however, held firm against the cavalry that was supposed to crush them, and by evening the whole army of Pompey had broken. The great general, who had once been called the greatest man in Rome, rode away from the camp in despair.

Pompey fled to Egypt, where he hoped to find shelter with the young king Ptolemy, but the royal advisers, who wished to please the victor, had him killed as he stepped ashore. When Caesar arrived a few days later, the messengers who brought him Pompey's head and ring expected to be rewarded, but he turned away and wept for the man who had been his friend and son-in-law. Plutarch adds that Caesar showed kindness to the friends of Pompey who had been captured, and that he was seen as a gentle victor.

At Alexandria the young Cleopatra, whose brother's advisers had driven her from the palace, saw that she had no hope unless she could speak to Caesar in person. She had a faithful servant named Apollodorus wrap her in a bed-sack and carry her past the guards, and Caesar, who was at first astonished, was soon completely won by her courage and wit. He arranged that she should rule jointly with her brother, and from that night the two were allies.

After a hard winter of fighting in the streets of Alexandria, Caesar left Egypt to Cleopatra and marched through Asia to deal with King Pharnaces, who had been taking advantage of the civil war. The battle at Zela in 47 BC was over in hours, and Caesar, who was always quick to turn a victory into a joke, wrote to a friend in Rome, “I came, I saw, I conquered.” The three words, which end alike in Latin, have had a swift and forceful ring ever since.

Once he had beaten the last of Pompey's supporters, Caesar returned to Rome as dictator and chose to be merciful, pardoning nearly all of those who had fought against him, and even giving some of them high office. He also found time for useful reforms, among them a new calendar, based on the sun, that was worked out with the help of astronomers and that is the ancestor of the one that we use today. Plutarch notes that the honours heaped on him by the Senate made many Romans uneasy.

At the festival of the Lupercalia in 44 BC, Mark Antony ran through the crowd and held out to the seated Caesar a crown of the sort that kings wore, and only a few of the onlookers applauded. Caesar pushed the crown away three times and sent it to the temple instead, and each time that he refused it, all the people cheered, though they were not entirely sure that he meant it. Soon afterwards he angrily dismissed two tribunes who had removed crowns from his statues, and the suspicion grew stronger.

A group of senators led by the bitter Cassius began to plot against Caesar, but they knew that their cause would never win public support unless the honest and thoughtful Brutus joined them. Notes were left on the judge's seat where Brutus sat in the city, saying, “You are asleep, Brutus,” and, since he was proud of his family's old hatred of kings, he gave way. Brutus, whom Caesar had pardoned and loved like a son, agreed with an aching heart that the freedom of Rome was more important than gratitude.

On the evening of March 14, at a dinner with friends, Caesar was asked which kind of death was best, and he answered, without looking up from his letters, that a sudden one was. That night his wife Calpurnia, who had never been afraid of dreams, groaned in her sleep, and in the morning she told him that she had seen his murdered body in her arms and begged him not to go out. The sacrifices that morning gave bad signs too, and Caesar, who was not well, began to think about staying at home.

Weeks before, a soothsayer named Spurinna had warned Caesar of danger until the Ides of March, but on that morning Decimus Brutus, a plotter, persuaded him to ignore his wife's dream and go to the Senate. Decimus argued that the senators, who had gathered at Caesar's own call, would be deeply insulted if he stayed away. On the way Caesar saw the soothsayer in the street and told him with a smile that the Ides had come, and the old man answered calmly, “Yes, but they have not yet gone.”

On the Ides of March 44 BC the plotters surrounded Caesar's chair in the Senate hall on the pretence of presenting a petition, and then, at a signal, they drew their daggers and struck at him from every side. Caesar defended himself for some time, but when he saw that Brutus too had drawn a blade, he gave up the struggle, drew his toga over his head and let himself fall at the foot of the statue of Pompey. He had suffered, it was said, twenty-three wounds, and the senators who were not in the plot fled in confusion.

At Caesar's funeral in the Forum, Mark Antony, who had learned how to move a crowd, held up the dead man's bloodstained robe and read aloud his will, which left a gift of money to every Roman citizen. The people, who had been quiet until then, were seized by anger and grief, burned the body in the Forum with the benches and tables of the market, and rushed through the streets looking for the killers. Brutus and Cassius, who had thought that Rome would thank them, were forced to flee the city within weeks.

Before the army of Brutus left Asia, a huge and terrible figure came into his tent at night and told him that it was his evil spirit and that he would see it at Philippi. In the autumn of 42 BC, at Philippi in northern Greece, Cassius killed himself after wrongly thinking that the day was lost, and Brutus, beaten in a second battle by Mark Antony and Octavian, followed him. Antony, who respected his noble enemy, laid his own purple cloak over the dead body.

Marcus Tullius Cicero was born in 106 BC in Arpinum, a small hill town, and his surname, from the Latin for chickpea, came from a forefather's cleft nose. When friends advised him to change it for the sake of his career, he swore that he would make the name more glorious than the greatest names in Rome. As a schoolboy he learned so quickly, according to Plutarch, that the fathers of other children came to watch him at his lessons.

As a young man Cicero had a thin, harsh voice and a delicate body, and his friends feared that the strain of speaking in public would damage his health. He therefore spent two years in Greece and Asia, studying philosophy in Athens and public speaking in Rhodes, where he learned to speak in a lower, steadier and more flexible tone. When he returned to Rome, his voice was well trained and his thinking was sharper than ever.

As an official in Sicily, Cicero governed with such fairness and kindness that the islanders never forgot it, and years afterwards they asked him to prosecute their former governor Verres, who had stolen from them on a grand scale. Cicero gathered so much evidence in so short a time that when the trial began in 70 BC, the defence was crushed, and Verres left the country before the verdict. The case made Cicero the leading speaker in Rome, and from then on the best cases in the city came to his door.

Cicero was elected consul in 63 BC, the highest office in Rome, and during his year he learned that a ruined nobleman named Catiline was gathering debtors and desperate men to seize the city by force. In a famous speech in the Senate, with Catiline sitting only a few feet away, Cicero asked him how much longer he intended to abuse the patience of Rome. The senators drew away from the conspirator, who realized that his plan had been found out.

Catiline left Rome during the night to join the rebel army that he had collected in the hills of Etruria, and he left behind a group of friends who were to burn the city and open its gates. Some Gaulish envoys, who had been approached by the plotters, told the authorities, and Cicero arranged for them to be given letters to carry so that the conspirators would be caught with proof in their own hands. Five of the chief plotters were arrested in the city and brought before the Senate.

In the Senate the great question was what should be done with the five prisoners, and Caesar warned that putting citizens to death without a trial would set a dangerous example and suggested life imprisonment. Cato answered him with a stirring speech, and the Senate, moved by fear and by his words, voted for execution, which Cicero carried out that same night. Soon afterwards the rebel army was beaten and Catiline died fighting, and the grateful Romans hailed Cicero as the father of his country.

Cicero's enemy Clodius, a clever and unscrupulous politician, persuaded the people to condemn him for putting Roman citizens to death without a trial, and in 58 BC Cicero left the city, mourning like a child in a foreign land. Plutarch is not kind about this period, observing that a man who could speak so boldly in the Senate behaved so weakly in his misfortune. Less than eighteen months later he was recalled, and the towns of Italy came out to cheer him on his way home.

When the civil war came, Cicero hesitated and then joined Pompey, but after the defeat at Pharsalus Caesar forgave him, and he returned to Rome to a quiet life. In 45 BC his dear daughter Tullia died, a loss that he felt more deeply than any political defeat, and in order to endure it he wrote books on philosophy, on the gods and on how to live. Many of those books survive and have been read by scholars and students ever since.

After Caesar's murder, Cicero attacked Mark Antony in a series of fiery speeches that he called the Philippics, in honour of the speeches by which Demosthenes had once warned Athens against Philip of Macedon. In the end Antony, Octavian and a third general named Lepidus made peace with one another and drew up a list of their enemies to be put to death, in which Antony demanded that Cicero's name be placed first. Octavian, who owed much to the old speaker, resisted for two days before he gave way.

Cicero tried to escape to the coast, and his servants carried him in a litter along a wooded road, but in December 43 BC Antony's soldiers caught up with him. Cicero put his head forward and told them to do their work, and afterwards Antony ordered that the head and hands of the great speaker be displayed in the Forum, where the Romans wept. Plutarch adds that years later Augustus found a grandson hiding a book by Cicero and said that he had been a learned man who loved his country.

After the victory at Philippi, Mark Antony, a bold, generous and pleasure-loving soldier, took the eastern half of the Roman world as his share and travelled from city to city collecting money for his armies. In 41 BC he summoned Cleopatra to the city of Tarsus, in what is now Turkey, to answer the charge that she had helped his enemies. Plutarch says that he thought the queen would come in fear, like any other ruler summoned by Rome.

Cleopatra did not come in fear, but sailed up the river Cydnus in a barge with a gilded stern, purple sails and silver oars that rose and fell to the music of flutes and pipes. She lay under a canopy of cloth of gold, dressed as Aphrodite, the goddess of love, with boys beside her fanning her like painted cupids, and perfumes drifted from the ship to both banks. The whole city ran to the river to see her, and Antony was left to sit alone in the market place.

Plutarch says that Cleopatra's beauty was not so remarkable that it astonished everyone, but that the charm of her talk, the sweetness of her voice and the force of her character made her company almost impossible to resist. She spoke with the Ethiopians, Arabs, Syrians and Parthians in their own languages, and she was the first of her family to take the trouble to learn Egyptian. Antony, who had been fond of the pleasures of life, was soon her willing captive.

Antony followed her to Alexandria, where he spent the winter in feasts, games and hunting, while his duties and even his wife in Italy were left far behind. Plutarch tells how once, when he was fishing without success, Cleopatra had a diver fasten a salted fish to his hook, and the whole court laughed when he pulled it up proudly in front of them. She told him to leave the rod to the rulers of small towns, because his game was cities, kingdoms and continents.

For a time Antony kept the peace with Octavian by marrying his sister Octavia, a gentle and respected woman who did all she could to keep the two men friends. In 36 BC, however, he led a great army against the Parthians in the east, and the campaign ended in a bitter winter retreat in which many thousands of his men died, after which he sought comfort in Egypt. Octavia, left behind in Rome, kept his house in order and cared for his children, even those whom his earlier wife Fulvia had borne him.

Octavian, who had long been waiting for a chance to ruin his rival, announced to the Romans the contents of Antony's will, which left lands to the children of Cleopatra and asked that his body should be buried in Alexandria. The citizens, already angry that Antony had divorced Octavia, felt that he had become a stranger to his own country, and they were glad to follow when Octavian proposed war. Rome declared war on Cleopatra in 32 BC, and both sides gathered fleets on the west coast of Greece.

In September 31 BC the two fleets met at the battle of Actium on the Greek coast, and for hours the struggle was equal, until Cleopatra's squadron suddenly hoisted its sails and made off for Egypt. Antony, who might still have won the day, jumped into a fast ship and followed her, and Plutarch recalls the old saying that a lover's soul lives in someone else's body. His army, left without orders, fought on for a time, and then, after a few days, it went over to Octavian.

When Octavian marched on Alexandria in 30 BC, Antony's last troops deserted him, and Cleopatra shut herself inside her tomb and let a rumour go out that she was dead. Believing it, Antony drove his sword into his own body, but he lived long enough to learn that she was alive, and his servants carried him to the tomb. Since the doors were sealed, Cleopatra and her women drew him up through a window with ropes, and he died in her arms, urging her to look after her own safety.

Octavian took Cleopatra prisoner and meant to lead her through Rome in his triumph, but she was determined not to be shown as a captive, and a few days later she was found dead in her royal robes. The story that she was killed by the bite of a snake, brought to her in a basket of figs, is the most famous, but Plutarch is honest enough to say that nobody knows the truth. Egypt, the last of the great kingdoms that Alexander's generals had founded, became a province of Rome, and Octavian returned to rule an empire.

Plutarch set each of his Greek heroes beside a Roman, Theseus beside Romulus, Demosthenes beside Cicero and Alexander beside Caesar, and he closed many of the pairs with a short comparison in which he weighed their virtues and their faults. His Lives were translated into English by Sir Thomas North in 1579, and from that book Shakespeare took the stories for Julius Caesar, Coriolanus and Antony and Cleopatra. Countless writers since have learned from Plutarch that character shows itself in small things, and his belief that a man is best known by a quiet word or a small act remains the best reason to go on reading him.
